### Round 534: DELETE /projects/:id could silently discard a concurrent mutation during its own WhatsApp-disconnect await

**The methodology**: following round 533's own closing suggestion (and the third-clean-round-in-a-row pattern that justified it), this round's Explore dispatch built and *ran* a real concurrency harness -- a genuine Express app (`createApp`) against a real in-memory SQLite DB, firing two truly concurrent HTTP requests via `Promise.all` of two real `fetch()` calls -- rather than reading code or unit-level fuzzing. This is exactly the methodology this process's history shows actually finds races (WhatsAppPanel round 530, idempotency rounds 495/528), unlike the prior three clean rounds.

**The finding**: `apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts`'s `DELETE /projects/:id` (then lines 620-631) checks `activePipelines.has(project.id)` but never *adds* to it, even though the route itself has a genuine async gap: `await whatsapp.disconnect(project.id)` (`apps/api/src/whatsappWeb.ts` line 363-379) awaits a real network round-trip (`sock.logout()`) whenever the project currently has a live WhatsApp Web connection -- an already-shipped, mainstream feature path, not a contrived edge case. Every ordinary quick mutation route in the same file (add a role, rename, add an entity, etc.) only *checks* `activePipelines`, never sets it, and has no other staleness guard. A request to any such route landing during DELETE's own await window reads the still-present project row, runs its entire read-modify-write to completion, and returns a normal-looking `200` with the "updated" project -- moments before `deleteProject()` erases the row (and that just-"persisted" change) with no error ever reaching the caller who got the 200.

**Independent verification**: read `DELETE /projects/:id` (lines 620-631) and its doc comment (590-619) directly -- confirmed it only *checks* `activePipelines`, matching the reported shape exactly. Read `whatsappWeb.ts`'s `disconnect()` directly -- confirmed the real `await session.sock.logout()` gap exists only when `session?.sock` is set (a genuinely connected session), and is otherwise skipped entirely. Read a racing partner (`POST /projects/:id/roles`, lines ~1273-1296) directly -- confirmed it calls `requireProjectAccess` (a single point-in-time existence check), checks `activePipelines` (which DELETE never sets), then `updateProjectSpec` straight through with no further existence re-check. Then independently wrote and ran my own fresh repro script (not copied from the subagent's) against the real `createApp()`/`createStore(":memory:")` harness, reusing this file's own `app.test.ts` test-double conventions (`createFakeWhatsAppSocket`, `createTestWhatsAppManager`) -- confirmed the race live, 5/5 trials: `DELETE status: 204 | POST /roles status: 200 | GET after status: 404 | role body had project: true` every time, with the role-add's full "successful" response body present moments before the project it referenced returned `404`.

**The fix**: `DELETE /projects/:id` now adds `project.id` to `activePipelines` for the duration of its own async work (the `whatsapp.disconnect()` await plus `deleteProject()`), in a `try`/`finally`, the exact same idiom `/build`, `/refine`, and `/answers` already use for themselves. No change was needed to any of the dozen+ racing routes' own `activePipelines.has()` checks -- they already existed and now correctly fire. Updated the route's own doc comment to describe this reverse-direction hazard alongside the pipeline-vs-delete hazard it already documented.

**The test**: one new regression test in `app.test.ts`, extending the existing `createFakeWhatsAppSocket`/`createTestWhatsAppManager` helpers with an optional, backward-compatible `logout` override (default behavior for every other existing test is unchanged). Holds `logout()` open with a controlled promise -- this file's own established technique for a deterministic race (not a real timer) -- waits for DELETE's own await to actually be entered (the same "wait for X to actually be entered" convention as round 424), then fires the concurrent `POST /roles` and asserts it now gets `409 PIPELINE_IN_PROGRESS` instead of a silently-discarded `200`, and that the delete itself still completes normally (`204`, final `GET` `404`).

**Regression-proof**: backed up `routes/projects.ts`, reverted it via `git checkout --` (keeping the new test in place), and confirmed the exact predicted failure: `200 !== 409`. Restored the file from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff`. Re-ran the new test against the restored code -- passed. Also re-ran my own independent (non-deterministic, real-timing) repro script against the restored code separately from the deterministic test: the race no longer reproduced in 5/5 trials (every trial now correctly returned `409` for the concurrent role-add). Full monorepo `npm test` (api 473/473, up from round 533's 472 by exactly the one new test; every other workspace unchanged: shared 16, spec-engine 116, db 149, web 875) and `npm run build` both clean. Commit `af29a10`.

**Topic status**: closed and pushed. No action needed from שלומי -- this only affects the narrow timing window where a project with a live WhatsApp connection is being deleted at almost the exact moment another action (a collaborator adding a role, renaming the project, etc.) touches it; that other action now correctly gets rejected with a clear error instead of silently losing its own result.

### Round 536: WhatsApp send could orphan a message row after a concurrent project delete

**The methodology**: continuing the concurrency-harness methodology that just found two real bugs in a row (534, 535), this round's Explore dispatch tried it against fresh routes/interactions outside the `activePipelines` family entirely, since both prior fixes had already closed that specific guard's gaps.

**The finding**: `POST /projects/:id/integrations/whatsapp/send` (`apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts`, lines 1041-1081) checks project access once, then does a genuine await -- `await whatsapp.sendMessage(project.id, to, message)`, a real network round-trip to the WhatsApp Web socket -- and only afterward unconditionally calls `insertWhatsAppMessage(db, {...})`. If a concurrent `DELETE /projects/:id` runs to completion while that await is still in flight, `deleteProject()` (`packages/db/src/projects.ts:226-241`) already purged that project's existing `whatsapp_messages` rows (`deleteWhatsAppData`) and removed the `projects` row itself, and the DELETE's own caller already got back `204` with a subsequent `GET` correctly `404`ing. The send route's write then still runs: since `whatsapp_messages.projectId` carries no foreign key (`packages/db/src/whatsapp.ts`'s `ensureWhatsAppMessagesTable`), the insert succeeds silently, creating a row for a project id that no longer exists anywhere -- permanently unreachable, since every reader route (`GET .../messages`, the backup ZIP, etc.) 404s via `requireProjectAccess` the instant the project is gone -- while the send request itself still reports `200 { ok: true }` as if nothing went wrong. This is the same bug class as rounds 534/535 (access-check, then a genuine await, then an unguarded write) in a third, independent route that was never in scope for either of those fixes (it has nothing to do with `project.spec`, so it correctly never touches `activePipelines` at all -- the fix needed here is a plain existence re-check after the await, not a lock).

### Round 537: DELETE /auth/account was not atomic across a user's own owned projects

**The methodology**: continuing the concurrency-harness methodology after three real-bug rounds in a row (534, 535, 536), this round's Explore dispatch tried it on `DELETE /auth/account` from a genuinely different angle than round 535's own fix to that same handler: not a second actor racing the handler, but the handler's *own* per-project loop failing non-atomically against its *own* `activePipelines` guard.

**The finding**: `DELETE /auth/account`'s per-owned-project cleanup loop (`apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts`, then lines 321-373) deleted projects one at a time and only checked `activePipelines` as each one was reached in the loop. If a user owned two or more projects and one of the *later* ones in `listOwnedProjectIds`' result happened to have a build/refine in flight, the loop would `throw` 409 on reaching it -- but every *earlier* project in the same loop had already been passed to `deleteProject()`, which is immediate and irreversible. Worse, `deleteAllSessionsForUser(db, req.userId!)` ran unconditionally at the very top of the handler, before the loop even started, so the user was fully logged out everywhere regardless of whether the rest of the operation succeeded. Net effect: a request that reports failure (`409 PIPELINE_IN_PROGRESS`) with the account itself still fully intact (re-login works, since `removeAllCollaborationsForUser`/`deleteUser` never ran) nonetheless *silently and irreversibly destroys* whichever of the user's other projects happened to be enumerated earlier in the loop -- a correctness/atomicity bug revealed by concurrency (an in-flight pipeline on one project while the account-deletion loop is mid-flight over several), not a TOCTOU race between two different requests like rounds 534/535/536.

**Independent verification**: read the current handler directly (post-round-535 shape, lines 321-373), confirming the exact per-iteration `if (activePipelines.has(projectId)) throw...` placement inside the loop and that `deleteAllSessionsForUser` runs unconditionally before it. Then wrote and ran my own independent repro script from scratch (not copied from the survey agent's) against the real `createApp()`/`createStore(":memory:")` harness: signed up an owner, created and built Project A, created and built Project B, started `POST /projects/:B/refine` with a custom `SpecProvider` whose `generate()` only hangs on a specific marker string (so A's and B's own creation/build calls, sharing the same provider, resolve immediately), waited for the hold to actually be entered (confirming `activePipelines` held B's id), then called `DELETE /auth/account` with the same owner token, released the hold, and checked what survived via a fresh login. Ran it 3/3 times -- every run produced `DELETE` status `409`, a successful re-login (account intact), Project A (processed first in the loop) `404` (gone), and Project B (the one whose guard aborted the loop) still `200` (untouched) -- the exact partial-destruction shape the finding describes.

**The fix**: check every owned project's `activePipelines` status up front, in one pass, before touching anything; if any is active, throw `409` immediately with nothing touched at all (sessions, projects, and the account all still intact). If the check passes, reserve every owned project id in `activePipelines` in the same synchronous pass (no `await` between the check and the reservation, so nothing else on this single-threaded process can interleave in between) *before* revoking sessions or deleting anything -- making the whole operation genuinely all-or-nothing, including against a pipeline that starts on a not-yet-reached project mid-loop (the gap the survey agent's own proposed fix left open, since it only checked-and-reserved as each project was reached rather than reserving all of them atomically up front).

**The test**: one new regression test in `app.test.ts`, reusing the file's existing `createGatedProvider()` helper (a controllable-gate `SpecProvider` already built for exactly this "block the next real AI/heuristic call deterministically" purpose) rather than inventing a new one -- `arm()` it only after both projects' own creation+build calls are done, so only the targeted `/refine` call blocks. Fires B's refine, waits for the gate to actually be entered, fires the account deletion, releases the gate, and asserts: the deletion is rejected with `409 PIPELINE_IN_PROGRESS`, a fresh login with the same credentials still succeeds, and both projects are still reachable afterward -- true all-or-nothing, not just "the account survives."

**Regression-proof**: backed up `routes/auth.ts`, reverted it via `git checkout --` (keeping the new test in place), and confirmed the exact predicted failure: `404 !== 200` for Project A. Restored the file from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff`. Re-ran the new test against the restored code -- passed. Full monorepo `npm test` (api 476/476, up from round 536's 475 by exactly the one new test; every other workspace unchanged: shared 16, spec-engine 116, db 149, web 875) and `npm run build` both clean. Commit `97353e4`.

**Topic status**: closed and pushed. No action needed from שלומי -- this only affects users who own two or more projects and happen to click "delete my account" at the exact moment one of those projects has a build/refine in flight; the request is now correctly all-or-nothing instead of silently destroying some of their data while reporting failure.

### Round 538: /auth/login's email-code step could invalidate a concurrent login's code before that login's own response was ever sent

**The methodology**: continuing the concurrency-harness methodology after four real-bug rounds in a row (534-537), this round's Explore dispatch was pointed at the same general shape (a guard-check/write pair not atomic around a genuine `await`, or a single handler's own multi-step loop failing non-atomically) but told to survey broadly for a new instance rather than revisiting `activePipelines` specifically, since that guard's own gaps (534, 535, 537) and its sibling access-check pattern (536) had all just been closed.

**The finding**: `POST /auth/login`'s email-code step (`apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts`, then lines 165-190) ran `deleteLoginCodesForUser(db, record.id)` + `createLoginCode(db, {...})` -- synchronously inserting the new pending-code row -- *before* its own genuine network await, `await emailSender.send(record.email, subject, body)` (a real HTTP call to Resend's API, `apps/api/src/email.ts`), and only then responded with `{ requiresCode: true, loginCodeId }`. `deleteLoginCodesForUser`'s own doc comment establishes the intended invariant ("at most one pending code per user ever exists"), and round 522's own test already confirmed this holds correctly for two *sequential* login calls. But two genuinely concurrent `POST /auth/login` calls for the same account (a double-click on "send code", a flaky-network client retry, two open tabs) overlap differently: whichever request's `send()` resolves chronologically second runs its own `deleteLoginCodesForUser` first, deleting the *other*, still in-flight request's already-inserted row -- while that other request is still parked on its own `send()`. When that first request's `send()` finally resolves, it responds with a `loginCodeId` already deleted out from under it. The user who receives that response, and who genuinely did just receive that exact code by email, gets a bare `401 LOGIN_CODE_EXPIRED` on their very first attempt even though nothing actually expired. This is reachable in the shipped product today -- round 522's own roadmap entry records that שלומי was asked to set `RESEND_API_KEY` on Render specifically to turn this code path on.

**Independent verification**: read the login handler directly (lines 140-194 at the time), confirming the exact ordering (synchronous write at lines 167-175, genuine `await emailSender.send(...)` at line 182, response at line 190), `loginCodes.ts`'s `deleteLoginCodesForUser`/`createLoginCode`/`getLoginCode` (confirmed each is a single, synchronous SQL statement with no intermediate await), and the `/auth/login/verify-code` route (confirmed a missing row reads as `LOGIN_CODE_EXPIRED`, indistinguishable from a genuinely expired one). Then wrote and ran my own independent repro script from scratch (a distinct gating design from the survey agent's own repro -- a "first-call-only" gate on `EmailSender.send` itself, the same idiom as this file's existing `createGatedProvider()` applied to a different dependency, rather than the agent's per-email-address gate) against the real `createApp()`/`createStore(":memory:")` harness: signed up an account, fired login request A (whose `send()` is the gate's first call and parks), waited for A's send to actually be entered (confirming A's own row was already inserted), fired login request B (whose `send()` is the gate's second call and resolves immediately, so B's own `deleteLoginCodesForUser` deletes A's row while A is still parked), released A's gate, and probed A's own returned `loginCodeId` with a deliberately wrong code (distinguishing `INVALID_LOGIN_CODE`, meaning the row still exists, from `LOGIN_CODE_EXPIRED`, meaning it's already gone -- without needing A's real 6-digit code). Ran it 3/3 times -- every run produced the bug: `LOGIN_CODE_EXPIRED` against A's own, never-yet-used `loginCodeId`.

**The fix**: reordered the handler so the write (`deleteLoginCodesForUser` + `createLoginCode`) happens only *after* `await emailSender.send(...)` succeeds, with no `await` between that write and `res.json(...)` -- the same "no await = no race" guarantee the rest of this codebase already relies on. On a `send()` failure, there is no longer a row to clean up at all (nothing was ever written), simplifying the existing `EMAIL_SEND_FAILED` error path as a side effect, and incidentally no longer invalidating a genuinely-still-valid previous code just because a *new* login attempt's email failed to send.

**The test**: one new regression test in `app.test.ts`, extending the existing `createFakeEmailSender` helper with a new optional, backward-compatible `gateFirstSend` option (every existing call site and test unaffected) that gates only the first `send()` call -- mirroring this file's own `createGatedProvider()` idiom, applied to `EmailSender` instead of `SpecProvider`. Fires login A, waits for A's send to actually be entered, fires login B to completion, releases A, and asserts: A and B minted two distinct `loginCodeId`s, and a wrong-code probe against A's own `loginCodeId` returns `INVALID_LOGIN_CODE` (row exists) rather than `LOGIN_CODE_EXPIRED` (row deleted out from under it).

**Regression-proof**: backed up `routes/auth.ts`, reverted it via `git checkout --` (keeping the new test in place), and confirmed the exact predicted failure: `LOGIN_CODE_EXPIRED !== INVALID_LOGIN_CODE`. Restored the file from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff`. Re-ran the new test against the restored code -- passed. Full monorepo `npm test` (api 477/477, up from round 537's 476 by exactly the one new test; every other workspace unchanged: shared 16, spec-engine 116, db 149, web 875) and `npm run build` both clean. Commit `21a2b41`.

**Topic status**: closed and pushed. No action needed from שלומי -- this only affects accounts with the optional email-code step turned on (`RESEND_API_KEY` set) in the narrow timing window where the same account's login is attempted twice in close succession (double-click, retry, two tabs); the first attempt's own code now survives correctly instead of being invalidated by the second attempt before the first's response was even sent.

### Round 539: PATCH /auth/password could report success after a concurrent account deletion silently dropped the write

**The methodology**: continuing the write-before/after-genuine-await methodology after five real-bug rounds in a row (534-538), this round's Explore dispatch was told explicitly that `routes/auth.ts` and `routes/projects.ts` had both been heavily mined for this exact bug class already, and to look specifically at a genuine *non-network* await -- scrypt password hashing, offloaded to libuv's threadpool (the same genuine-yield mechanism this file's own pre-existing "two concurrent signups" test, added before this round's methodology even started, already relies on) -- as a less-mined source of the same bug shape.

**The finding**: `PATCH /auth/password` (`apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts`, then lines 279-299) ran `verifyPassword` then `hashPassword` -- both genuine awaits, each offloaded to libuv's threadpool specifically so "the event loop stays free to service other requests while a hash computes" (`auth/password.ts`'s own doc comment) -- and only then wrote `updatePasswordHash` and `deleteOtherSessionsForUser` unconditionally, responding `204`. Both of those writes are plain `UPDATE`/`DELETE ... WHERE userId = ?` statements that silently affect zero rows if the user is already gone -- no error, no indication anything went wrong. A concurrent `DELETE /auth/account` using the SAME still-valid session token (two tabs/devices, or any client-side retry firing both) could pass its own `requireAuth` check before `deleteAllSessionsForUser` (inside that handler) ever revoked anything, then run almost entirely synchronously to completion -- deleting the user row -- while `PATCH /auth/password` was still parked on one of its own scrypt awaits. When PATCH resumed, both of its writes silently no-op'd, yet it still responded `204` as if the password change had genuinely succeeded on an account that, at that exact moment, no longer existed anywhere. This is the same bug shape as rounds 534-538 (a genuine await creates a window for a second request to invalidate the first's premise before its writes/response), but it's the first instance in this series found between two routes racing EACH OTHER'S *own* user (the same "account owner's own concurrent requests" shape as rounds 535/537, not a stranger/collaborator), and the first found via a CPU-offloaded await rather than a network-bound one.

**Independent verification**: read `PATCH /auth/password` directly (lines 279-299), `auth/password.ts`'s `hashPassword`/`verifyPassword` (confirming both are genuinely offloaded via `promisify(scrypt)`, per the file's own doc comment), `updatePasswordHash`/`deleteOtherSessionsForUser`/`findUserById` (`packages/db/src/users.ts`, confirming the first two are silent no-ops on a missing row and the third is already imported in `routes/auth.ts` for `/auth/login/verify-code`'s own identical "account vanished" check), and `DELETE /auth/account`'s current (post-round-537) shape, confirming `deleteAllSessionsForUser` runs synchronously at the very top of its try block, before any of its own awaits. Then wrote and ran my own independent repro script from scratch (not copied from the survey agent's) against the real `createApp()`/`createStore(":memory:")` harness: signed up a user, fired a couple of throwaway warm-up requests to settle HTTP connection-setup jitter, fired `PATCH /auth/password` with a real current/new password pair, gave it a 20ms head start (long enough for its own `requireAuth` and `verifyPassword`'s scrypt call to have genuinely begun), then fired `DELETE /auth/account` with the same token, and finally queried the `users` table directly for ground truth. Ran it 3/3 times -- every run produced the bug: `DELETE` `204`, `PATCH` *also* `204`, yet the user row was confirmed gone from the database.

**The fix**: after the last genuine await (`hashPassword`) and before the first write, added a synchronous `findUserById` existence re-check; if the account is gone, respond `401 USER_NOT_FOUND` instead of writing and responding `204` -- mirroring the exact pattern already established for `POST /projects/:id/integrations/whatsapp/send`'s post-await re-check (round 536) and `findUserById`'s existing use for the identical case in `/auth/login/verify-code`. No new guard/Set needed -- there's no pipeline concept for a plain password change, just a plain existence check with no await between it and the writes it gates.

**The test**: one new regression test in `app.test.ts`, following this file's own pre-existing "two concurrent signups" idiom (no artificial gate -- real wall-clock overlap from scrypt's genuine threadpool offload) rather than inventing a controlled-promise mechanism: signs up, fires `PATCH /auth/password` with a short head start, fires `DELETE /auth/account` with the same token, and asserts PATCH responds `401 USER_NOT_FOUND` (never `204`) and that the email is free to re-register afterward (proving the account was genuinely, cleanly deleted, not left half-updated).

**Regression-proof**: backed up `routes/auth.ts`, reverted it via `git checkout --` (keeping the new test in place), and confirmed the exact predicted failure: `204 === 204` where the test expects not-204. Restored the file from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff`. Re-ran the new test against the restored code -- passed. Full monorepo `npm test` (api 478/478, up from round 538's 477 by exactly the one new test; every other workspace unchanged: shared 16, spec-engine 116, db 149, web 875) and `npm run build` both clean. Commit `97b1c94`.

**Topic status**: closed and pushed. No action needed from שלומי -- this only affects the narrow timing window where someone changes their password at almost the exact moment they (or a second device/tab under their account) delete the account itself; the password-change request now correctly reports failure instead of falsely claiming success on data that no longer exists.

### Round 540: self-referencing relation picker could lose a just-created record to a slower mount-time fetch

**The methodology**: after six write-before/after-await rounds in a row (534-539) had very heavily mined `routes/auth.ts` and `routes/projects.ts`, this round's Explore dispatch was told explicitly NOT to just re-run the same playbook on the same two files, and to spend real effort looking broadly first -- a genuinely different bug class, or the same race mechanism on genuinely unexplored ground (including client-side, per the round 431-433 precedent that two independent fetches/effects in a React component is a different, still-legitimate race mechanism from the server-side one).

**The finding**: `EntityPanel.tsx`'s mount-time `loadRelated` effect (then lines 922-945) and its `refresh()` function (round 438's own fix) were two independent writers of the *same* `relatedRecords[entity.name]` slot for a self-referencing relation field (e.g. `Category.parentCategoryId -> Category`). `refresh()` -- called by every create/edit/delete/duplicate/bulk-update/CSV-import/board-move/inline-edit handler -- merges a newly-created same-entity record into that slot immediately, which is exactly what round 438 added. But `loadRelated` independently *also* fetches `entity.name`'s own records at mount (since it's one of the entity's own `relationTargets`) and, when its fetch resolves, unconditionally replaces the *entire* `relatedRecords` object with its own snapshot -- not just merges it. If that mount-time fetch happens to resolve *after* `refresh()` has already merged a freshly-created record in (a perfectly ordinary case: the initial page-load fetch is even slightly slower than a fast subsequent create), `loadRelated`'s own stale, pre-creation snapshot wholesale-overwrites `relatedRecords`, silently undoing round 438's fix the moment this ordinary timing occurs -- the user creates a new category, picks it as a parent for another record, and watches it vanish from the dropdown again a moment later with no further action on their part. Round 438 only ever asked "does `refresh()` update `relatedRecords` at all" (it didn't, before that fix) and never considered that `loadRelated` remained a second, competing writer of the exact same key; rounds 440 and 515 are a different code path entirely (`FieldInput`'s own fallback rendering for a missing/failed-fetch related record, not this cross-effect write race).

**Independent verification**: read `loadRelated` and `refresh()` directly (lines 915-1010 at the time), confirming both are independently triggered at mount (`loadRelated` keyed on `[projectId, relationTargets]`, `refresh()`'s own effect keyed on `[entity.name]`), both issue a GET to the exact same `/api/projects/:id/entities/:name` endpoint for a self-referencing entity, and `loadRelated`'s own `setRelatedRecords(Object.fromEntries(entries))` call is a full replace with no merge against whatever `refresh()` may have already written. Then wrote and ran my own independent regression test from scratch, added directly to `EntityPanel.test.ts` (reusing the file's own established `withJsdom`/`renderEntityPanel`/`waitForCondition` harness and the exact `Category`/self-relation fixture from round 438's adjacent existing test, rather than copying the survey agent's standalone-script repro): a fetch mock that holds open only the *first* GET to the Category endpoint (modeling whichever of the two competing mount-time fetches happens to start first) while letting every later request -- including the other effect's own mount GET and the subsequent create's POST+refetch -- resolve immediately; creates "Office Supplies", confirms it's correctly selectable right after creation (round 438's own invariant), releases the held GET, and checks whether it's *still* selectable afterward. Ran against the then-current code: failed exactly as predicted -- `"Office Supplies"` present right after creation, then gone once the delayed fetch resolved (`got options: Choose…, Electronics`).

**The fix**: in `loadRelated`, excluded `entity.name` from the set of relation targets this effect actually fetches over the network when the entity is self-referencing (`otherTargets = relationTargets.filter((name) => name !== entity.name)`), and when applying its results, merged in whatever `refresh()` has already written for `entity.name` (`setRelatedRecords((prev) => ({ ...Object.fromEntries(entries), ...(isSelfReferencing ? { [entity.name]: prev[entity.name] } : {}) }))`), instead of replacing the whole object. This makes `refresh()` the sole writer of that one key -- `loadRelated` can structurally never again overwrite it with a stale snapshot, regardless of timing, closing the race entirely rather than narrowing its window. The non-self-referencing case (the overwhelming majority of entities) is untouched: `otherTargets` equals the original `relationTargets` list and the merge spread contributes nothing.

**The test**: one new regression test in `EntityPanel.test.ts`, right after round 438's own adjacent test, as described above under independent verification -- it doubles as both my own verification and the permanent regression guard.

**Regression-proof**: backed up `EntityPanel.tsx`, reverted it via `git checkout --` (keeping the new test in place), and confirmed the exact predicted failure (`"Office Supplies"` missing from the options after the delayed fetch resolved). Restored the file from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff`. Re-ran the new test against the restored code -- passed. Full monorepo `npm test` (web 876/876, up from round 539's 875 by exactly the one new test; every other workspace unchanged: shared 16, spec-engine 116, db 149, api 478) and `npm run build` both clean. Commit `d2b1dca`.

**Topic status**: closed and pushed. No action needed from שלומי -- this only affects entities with a self-referencing relation field (e.g. a "parent category" or "manager" picker pointing back at the same entity) in the narrow timing window where the initial page load's own data fetch is slower than a subsequent create of a same-entity record; the newly-created record now stays correctly selectable regardless of that timing.

### Round 541: WhatsApp panel's mount-time message fetch could resurrect messages the user had just disconnected away from

**The methodology**: following round 540's own finding that client-side competing-writer races are a legitimate, still-unmined territory now that `routes/auth.ts`/`routes/projects.ts` are heavily exhausted, this round's Explore dispatch was told to look for the same race *mechanism* (two independent writers of one state slot) in a *different* React component, or run a completely fresh general survey with no fixed assumption about where the next bug lies.

**The finding**: `WhatsAppPanel.tsx` already has an established, well-documented idiom (`messagesVersionRef`, added in round 530 after rounds 431/432 found the same gap in two other call sites) for exactly this shape of bug: every call site that fetches `listWhatsAppMessages` and later calls `setMessages`/`setHasMoreMessages` is supposed to capture the version before its own fetch starts and skip applying the result if something else (a disconnect or a clear) bumped the version while it was in flight. `loadInitialStatus`'s own "already connected when the panel mounts" branch (then lines 347-364) was the one remaining `listWhatsAppMessages` call site with no such guard at all -- every sibling call site (`startPolling`'s "becoming connected" branch, `startConnectedPolling`'s tick, `handleSendTest`, `handleRetry`, `handleLoadMore`) already had it. Mounting the panel while WhatsApp is already connected (an entirely ordinary case -- reopening the panel, or any fresh page load while already linked from a previous session) kicks off this unguarded fetch. If the user clicks "Disconnect" before it resolves, `handleDisconnect` bumps `messagesVersionRef`, sets status to disconnected, and explicitly clears the log (`setMessages([])`) -- but `loadInitialStatus`'s own fetch, with no guard, would still unconditionally overwrite that just-cleared empty log with the stale, pre-disconnect page once it resolved, directly undoing `handleDisconnect`'s own documented intent.

**Independent verification**: read `loadInitialStatus`, `handleDisconnect`, and the `messagesVersionRef` doc comment directly (lines 203-221, 347-364, 404-432 at the time), confirming every other `listWhatsAppMessages`/`setMessages` pairing in the file already captures and re-checks the version and that `loadInitialStatus`'s connected-branch fetch was the sole exception -- confirmed via a full-file grep of every `listWhatsAppMessages` call site. Then wrote and ran my own independent regression test from scratch in `WhatsAppPanel.test.ts`, reusing this file's own established "extract the real function via regex, strip TypeScript with esbuild, run it in isolation with mocked dependencies via `new Function`" idiom (the same technique round 530's own adjacent `startPolling` race test uses) rather than a full React render: mocked `getWhatsAppStatus` to resolve "connected" immediately and `listWhatsAppMessages` to hold open until released, called the extracted `loadInitialStatus`, waited for its fetch to actually start, bumped `messagesVersionRef` (simulating `handleDisconnect`'s own bump), released the held fetch, and asserted `setMessages`/`setHasMoreMessages` were never called. Ran against the then-current code: failed exactly as predicted (`setMessagesCalls` was `1`, not the expected `0`).

**The fix**: in `loadInitialStatus`'s connected branch, captured `messagesVersionRef.current` into `versionBeforeFetch` immediately before calling `listWhatsAppMessages`, and added `if (messagesVersionRef.current !== versionBeforeFetch) return;` as the first line of that fetch's `.then` callback, before `setMessages`/`setHasMoreMessages` -- the identical idiom already used by every sibling call site in this file. `startConnectedPolling()`, which runs unconditionally right after kicking off the fetch (not inside the `.then`), is deliberately left unguarded, matching its own existing behavior at every other call site.

**The test**: one new regression test in `WhatsAppPanel.test.ts`, inserted right after round 530's own adjacent `startPolling` race test, as described above under independent verification -- it doubles as both my own verification and the permanent regression guard.

**Regression-proof**: backed up `WhatsAppPanel.tsx`, reverted it via `git checkout --` (keeping the new test in place), and confirmed the exact predicted failure (`setMessagesCalls` `1 !== 0`). Restored the file from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff`. Re-ran the new test against the restored code -- passed, and the full `WhatsAppPanel.test.ts` file (35/35) also passed clean. Full monorepo `npm test` (web 877/877, up from round 540's 876 by exactly the one new test; every other workspace unchanged: shared 16, spec-engine 116, db 149, api 478) and `npm run build` both clean. Commit `b996e5f`.

### Round 542: deleting an account before its own project-id fetch resolved could silently orphan localStorage forever

**The methodology**: following round 541's finding that an existing guard idiom missing from one call site is a legitimate bug shape distinct from "two effects both writing," this round's Explore dispatch was told to look for the same shape in a genuinely different file/guard, another client-side competing-effects race in a different component, or a completely fresh general survey.

**The finding**: `DeleteAccountPanel.tsx`'s mount effect fires an independent `listMyProjectIds()` fetch and only later (in its `.then`) sets `ownedProjectIds`/`sharedProjectIds` state, initialized to `[]`. `handleSubmit` (then lines 75-87) is a plain closure over whatever those two arrays happen to be in state *at the moment of submission* -- its only gate was `canSubmit`, whether the typed confirmation text matches the account's own email; nothing tied submission to the id-fetch having resolved, and the submit button's `disabled` prop (`busy || !canSubmit`) carried the same gap through to the UI. If a user who already knows their own email (or has it in a password manager/clipboard) opens the panel and submits before that fetch resolves -- a real, plausible network race, not a contrived one -- `handleSubmit` reads the still-initial `[]` arrays, calls the real `deleteAccount()` (which succeeds and genuinely deletes every owned project and revokes every shared collaboration server-side, exactly as designed), and then calls `onDeleted([], [])`. `App.tsx`'s `handleAccountDeleted` (lines 1287-1304) trusts whatever arrays it's handed and loops `purgeProjectPreferences` over them -- with both arrays empty, it sweeps nothing, so every one of the ~18 projectId-keyed localStorage preference stores belonging to the just-deleted projects sits in this browser forever, under an account that can never log back in to clean them up. This is the same "leaked localStorage preferences" symptom rounds 403/423/510 already fixed -- but those three rounds only ever hardened *what* `onDeleted` is eventually called with once the fetch resolves; none of them gated *when* submission is allowed to happen relative to that fetch completing.

**Independent verification**: read `DeleteAccountPanel.tsx` in full (the mount effect, `canSubmit`, `handleSubmit`, and the submit button's `disabled` prop) and `App.tsx`'s `handleAccountDeleted`, confirming the gap traced exactly as described -- the submit button's only gating really was `busy || !canSubmit`, with no reference anywhere to whether the id-fetch had settled. Noted that the file's own first existing test (`DeleteAccountPanel.test.ts`, "typing the account's own email exactly and submitting...") already exercises this exact early-submit ordering (types and submits back-to-back with no wait for the mount fetch) but only asserts `onDeleted` fired at all, never checking what ids it received, so it passed without ever noticing the arrays were empty. Then wrote and ran my own independent regression test from scratch, holding the `GET /api/projects/mine-ids` fetch open with a controlled promise (this file's first use of that idiom; every other existing test in it resolves immediately) so the submit attempt could land deterministically while the fetch was still in flight. Ran against the then-current code: failed exactly as predicted -- the submit button was not disabled while the fetch was still in flight (`expected: true, actual: false`).

**The fix**: added a new `idsFetchSettled` state flag, set via `.finally()` on the mount-time `listMyProjectIds()` call so it becomes `true` once the fetch settles either way (success or failure) -- deliberately kept separate from `projectSummary` (which stays `null` on a failed fetch too, for display purposes only) so a failed fetch never permanently blocks a user from deleting their own account. `handleSubmit` now returns early if `!idsFetchSettled`, and the submit button's `disabled` prop was extended to `busy || !canSubmit || !idsFetchSettled`, closing the race at both the logic level (so a bypassed-disabled submission, e.g. via Enter, still no-ops) and the UI level.

**The test**: one new regression test in `DeleteAccountPanel.test.ts`, described above under independent verification, that both proves the bug and guards against it: asserts the submit button stays disabled and that submitting while the fetch is held open never calls `DELETE /auth/account` or fires `onDeleted`, then releases the held fetch and confirms the submission now succeeds with the real (non-empty) owned/shared ids. Also updated two pre-existing tests ("typing the account's own email exactly and submitting...", "a server error is shown to the user...") that previously submitted immediately with no wait, adding a wait for the submit button to become enabled first -- the same signal a real user waits on, and now a genuine behavioral requirement rather than just a timing nicety.

**Regression-proof**: backed up `DeleteAccountPanel.tsx`, reverted it via `git checkout --` (keeping the new and updated tests in place), and confirmed the exact predicted failure in the new test. Restored the file from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff`. Re-ran the full `DeleteAccountPanel.test.ts` file against the restored code -- all 10 tests passed clean. Full monorepo `npm test` (web 878/878, up from round 541's 877 by exactly the one new test; every other workspace unchanged: shared 16, spec-engine 116, db 149, api 478) and `npm run build` both clean. Commit `b5c4ce4`.

**Topic status**: closed and pushed. No action needed from שלומי -- this only affects the narrow timing window where someone submits the account-deletion confirmation faster than the project-list fetch that started when the panel opened; a legitimate account deletion now always sweeps the right projects' localStorage entries regardless of that timing, and a failed id-fetch no longer blocks deletion at all.

### Round 543: double-clicking "Delete Selected" reported a fully successful bulk delete as a failure

**The methodology**: following round 542's finding that the same bug shape (an action handler not gated on a relevant async operation having settled) can recur in a brand-new guard rather than a missing call site on an existing one, this round's Explore dispatch was told to look for the same shape in a different component, another client-side competing-effects race, or a completely fresh general survey.

**The finding**: `App.tsx`'s `handleBulkDeleteProjects` (the home screen's "Delete Selected" bulk-action button) has no busy-tracking state at all, unlike every other mutating action on that same screen -- `deletingId` and `cloningId` both gate their own single-row buttons via a `disabled` prop, but the "Delete Selected" button (then line 1488) had no `disabled` attribute and never changed its label. Between the `await window.confirm(...)` and the `await Promise.allSettled(ids.map(deleteProject))` call, the function is suspended for the full round trip of N real `DELETE` requests -- during that entire window `selectedProjectIds` is untouched, so the bulk-actions bar and its button stay fully visible and clickable. A second click before the first batch resolves starts a second, fully independent invocation with the exact same `ids`, firing a second round of `DELETE` requests for projects the first batch is already in the middle of deleting. The first batch's requests win and succeed (`204`); the second batch's requests each hit a 404 (`requireProjectOwner` -- the row is already gone) or 409 `PIPELINE_IN_PROGRESS` (`routes/projects.ts`'s own `activePipelines` guard, if it lands during the first batch's own `whatsapp.disconnect()`/`deleteProject()` window) -- never a success. Back on the client, that losing batch's own `Promise.allSettled` sees every entry rejected, so it reports `failedIds.length === ids.length` and shows the *first* rejection's message as if the whole bulk delete had failed, and re-marks every id "selected" again via `setSelectedProjectIds(new Set(failedIds))` -- even though every one of those projects had, in fact, already been deleted by the winning first batch moments earlier. The user is told their delete failed for an action that fully succeeded, exactly the kind of false negative that could prompt a worried retry or a belief that data wasn't actually removed.

**Independent verification**: read `handleBulkDeleteProjects` and its button directly, confirming no busy state existed anywhere in the function or its JSX, and diffed against the two sibling single-row actions (`deletingId`/`cloningId`) in the very same file that already have the guard. Read `routes/projects.ts`'s `DELETE /projects/:id` to confirm the server-side shape of the race's outcome (404 via `requireProjectOwner`, or 409 `PIPELINE_IN_PROGRESS` via `activePipelines`, never a silent no-op). Separately confirmed `EntityPanel.tsx`'s own, differently-named `handleBulkDelete` is NOT vulnerable to the same shape: its entire body up through `setSelectedIds(new Set())` runs synchronously (the real network calls are deferred behind a `setTimeout`-based undo window), so a second click can't interleave mid-function the way an `async`/`await`-suspended handler can -- the same "no await = no race" distinction this project's own rounds 423/424 established. Then wrote and ran my own independent regression test from scratch in `App.test.ts`, extracting the real `handleBulkDeleteProjects` (the same regex-extraction idiom the file's own two pre-existing bulk-delete tests already use) and modeling a real re-render: constructing a fresh handler closure bound to the current `bulkDeleteBusy` value each "click," exactly as a real `onClick` prop is rebound on every render. Ran against the then-current code: failed exactly as predicted -- `bulkDeleteBusy` never became `true` after the first invocation began (`false !== true`), since the flag didn't exist yet.

**The fix**: added a new `bulkDeleteBusy` boolean state, mirroring the existing `deletingId`/`cloningId` idiom. `handleBulkDeleteProjects` returns early if already busy, sets the flag before its own `Promise.allSettled` and clears it in a `finally` block (so the flag can never get stuck `true` after an error), and the button's `disabled` prop and label now reflect it, matching the two sibling single-row buttons.

**The test**: one new regression test in `App.test.ts`, described above under independent verification, that proves and guards against the race: starts a first (held-open) bulk delete, confirms it marks itself busy and begins both deletes, then simulates a second click landing while the first is still in flight and confirms it's a complete no-op (no second confirmation prompt, no second `deleteProject` calls), then releases the first batch and confirms it completes normally with no error. Also updated the file's two pre-existing `handleBulkDeleteProjects` tests to inject the new `bulkDeleteBusy`/`setBulkDeleteBusy` parameters the extracted function now references (both otherwise unaffected -- they still pass unchanged against the old code too).

**Regression-proof**: backed up `App.tsx`/`language.ts`, reverted them via `git checkout --` (keeping all test changes in place), and confirmed the exact predicted failure in the new test (and only that test -- 68/69 passed against the old code, the two updated pre-existing tests included). Restored the files from backup, confirmed byte-identical via `diff`. Re-ran the full `App.test.ts` file against the restored code -- all 69 tests passed clean. Full monorepo `npm test` (web 879/879, up from round 542's 878 by exactly the one new test; every other workspace unchanged: shared 16, spec-engine 116, db 149, api 478) and `npm run build` both clean. Commit `5916092`.

**Topic status**: closed and pushed. No action needed from שלומי -- this only affects the narrow case of clicking "Delete Selected" twice in quick succession on a multi-project selection; a bulk delete that genuinely succeeds now always reports success, regardless of that timing.

### Round 544: double-clicking "Duplicate selected" or the bulk-update "Apply" button in an entity's record table started a second, independent batch

**The methodology**: this is now the third consecutive round finding the identical bug shape (an async bulk-action handler with no busy guard, sitting right next to a sibling handler that already has one) in a different file each time -- `DeleteAccountPanel.tsx` (round 542) → `App.tsx`'s "Delete Selected" (round 543) → this round's `EntityPanel.tsx`. The Explore dispatch was told to keep looking for the same shape anywhere it hadn't yet been checked.

**The finding**: `EntityPanel.tsx`'s `handleBulkDuplicate` ("Duplicate selected") and `handleBulkUpdate` (the bulk-edit "Apply to N" button) -- the per-entity record table's own bulk actions, distinct from the home screen's project-level bulk delete round 543 just fixed -- had no busy state and no `disabled` attribute on their buttons, while the very same component's `handleBulkDelete` right next to them was already safe, for the same "no await before the synchronous state clear" reason round 543 established. Both vulnerable handlers only touch `selectedIds` *after* their own `Promise.allSettled` resolves, so the buttons stayed clickable for the full round trip of N real `createRecord`/`updateRecord` calls. A second click during that window started a fully independent second batch for the same selected ids -- double-clicking "Duplicate selected" created two copies of every selected record instead of one; double-clicking "Apply" sent the same field update twice per record.

Each proves the first click marks itself busy and starts its own calls, a second click while still in flight makes zero additional calls, and releasing the first lets it finish normally with the busy flag cleared and no error. Also updated the four pre-existing `EntityPanel.test.ts` tests and three pre-existing `codegen.test.ts` call sites that extract and invoke these handlers via `new Function(...)`, injecting the new `bulkActionBusy`/`setBulkActionBusy` parameters they now reference (all otherwise unaffected).
