### Round 776: two open questions sharing identical wording collided -- the second question's answer always silently overwrote the first, at the wire-format level, before either reached the server

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey was explicitly steered away from WhatsApp, Automations/Time Machine, and the just-added personas section (rounds 770-775), and found that `openQuestions` -- the one spec-level array still missing any defense against its own text colliding -- had the exact same root-cause shape as the many field/entity-label collision bugs this routine has repeatedly had to fix, just never caught here.

**The gap**: `POST /projects/:id/answers`' `AnswerQuestionsSchema.answers` (`apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts`) was a flat `Record<string,string>` keyed by the open question's own `question` text, and the client's `selectedAnswers` state (`apps/web/src/App.tsx`) used the identical keying. `OpenQuestionSchema` (`packages/shared/src/index.ts`) carries no uniqueness constraint on `question` -- unlike entity names, which get a real case-insensitive collision `.refine()` a few lines below it in the very same `ProductSpecSchema` -- and the AI provider's own system prompt (`packages/spec-engine/src/anthropic.ts`) gives the model no reason to avoid asking two unrelated questions with identical wording (e.g. two different features each independently prompting "Should notifications be sent via email or SMS?"). A plain JS object cannot hold two entries under the same key, so the second question's answer always silently overwrote the first's in the request body itself -- before the server's own code even ran. On screen, both questions' chips and free-text inputs read from the same `selectedAnswers` slot, so answering one instantly (and wrongly) showed the other as already answered too, and the "answered N of M" progress line double-counted a single click.

**Why this is not deliberate**: this is the identical bug *class* the codebase has repeatedly retrofitted real fixes for elsewhere -- field-label collisions in `AutomationsPanel`/`automationsReport`/`calendarIcs`/`twin.ts`/`entityFormatting.ts`, entity-label collisions, relation source-label collisions in `twin.ts`'s `computeRelationHubObservation` -- every one of those got a disambiguation fix once discovered. `openQuestions` had no such treatment and no schema-level uniqueness guard, unlike entities. The heuristic (offline) provider never generates more than one open question, so this gap is reachable only through the AI path -- but that's the primary, intended path for real user ideas, and nothing in the schema or prompt prevents it.

**The fix**: `answers` is now an array of `{question, answer}` pairs, not a keyed object, so two identically-worded questions each keep their own distinct answer through the full round trip. The client keys `selectedAnswers` by each question's own array index instead of its text, and `handleBuild` pairs each index's answer back to its real question text when building the array to send to the server.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- grepped `codegen.ts` for `openQuestion`/`selectedAnswers`: no matches. The exported standalone app has no Spec Review screen at all (by export time the spec is already built/frozen).

**The tests**: updated 4 existing API tests and 7 existing web tests to the new array/index shape. Added a new API test that writes a spec with two identically-worded open questions directly via `updateProjectSpec` (simulating what a real AI-generated spec can produce, since the heuristic provider can't) and confirms both answers reach the regeneration prompt as distinct lines, via a capturing provider wrapper. Added two new web tests: one confirming `countAnsweredOpenQuestions` counts two identically-worded questions independently by position, and one confirming `handleBuild`'s own real source (extracted and run directly, this file's established pattern for testing App.tsx handlers) sends each question's own answer as a distinct pair instead of collapsing them.

**Verification**: reverted three different fix sites in turn -- the route's array-to-Record collapse, `handleBuild`'s index-based answer lookup, and `countAnsweredOpenQuestions`' index-based filter -- and reran the corresponding new test each time; all three failed exactly as predicted, then were restored and reran clean. Full `app.test.ts` (223/223) and `App.test.ts` (81/81) both pass. Both workspaces changed this round, so both full suites ran: `apps/api` 545/546 (the sole failure, `codegen.test.ts` at `:1:1`, is the long-documented pre-existing exit-hang flake, now confirmed unrelated across 19+ rounds); `apps/web` 1090/1090, no flakes. `tsc -b` (apps/web) and `npm run build` (apps/api's esbuild bundle) both clean.

### Round 780: "Group by" kept grouping by a field a live refine had retyped, silently mislabeling every record under a fabricated "Yes" group

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's first survey re-proposed `migrate.ts`'s long-closed "case-only entity rename" candidate (already explicitly rejected in rounds 626 and 635 as tautological -- no stable entity ID exists anywhere in the system, so a genuine rename and a remove-then-unrelated-readd-with-colliding-case are structurally indistinguishable from the spec data alone); independently re-verified and declined again without touching any code, and a second survey was launched with that topic marked off-limits. It returned a genuinely new, well-evidenced finding in a different file.

**The gap**: `groupFieldName`'s own load effect (`apps/web/src/EntityPanel.tsx`) only re-validated on a project/entity *switch* (`[projectId, entity.name]`) -- it never re-ran while staying mounted on the same entity through a live refine, so a field whose TYPE changes while its NAME survives (e.g. an enum `"status"` refined into a `boolean`) kept the exact same grouping selection. `groupRecordsByField`'s boolean/relation branches have no "legacy value" guard the way the enum branch's own `"(other)"` bucket already does: a pre-existing record's stale old-type value (a leftover enum string like `"Shipped"`) coerces through `Boolean(...)` to `true`, so every record except a genuinely-empty one landed in a single, confidently-labeled "Yes" group, with real per-group subtotals computed over that fabricated split -- no error, no visible sign anything was wrong.

**Why this is not deliberate**: this is the identical "field TYPE changes while NAME survives" bug class round 751 already fixed for the sibling `fieldFilters` state -- and that same round *deliberately declined* to extend the fix to `sortKeys`, reasoning that sorting by a retyped field's raw value is merely "harmless, visually odd at worst." That stated exemption does not hold for `groupFieldName`: grouping doesn't just reorder rows, it buckets them under confident literal labels and computes real subtotals, structurally much closer to the `fieldFilters` case round 751 *did* fix than to the `sortKeys` case it declined.

**The fix**: unlike `fieldFilters`' own stored *value* (whose shape can be checked directly against the field's current type, no memory needed), `groupFieldName` is just a field *name* with no shape to check against a type. A `ref` now remembers the type of whichever field `groupFieldName` currently names, captured the moment it's chosen (by the user, or reloaded from storage), and the selection is cleared via the existing round-462 clearing path (which also resets persisted storage) the moment that type changes out from under it -- also closing the "stale value has no `<option>`" blank-select hazard for the case a type change moves the field *out* of being groupable entirely.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- the exported standalone app's `groupFieldName` is a plain `useState` lazy initializer with no live-refine re-validation concept at all (its entity list is baked in once at generation time), the same reasoning round 751 used to rule out codegen.ts parity for its own identical fix.

**The tests**: added a new DOM test mirroring round 751's own `fieldFilters` type-change test exactly -- groups a Deal entity's table by an enum `status` field with two real records, then rerenders (no remount, same `entity.name`) with `status` retyped to boolean, and confirms the grouping is dropped entirely (dropdown resets to "no grouping", table renders flat) rather than mislabeling both records under a fabricated "Yes" group.

**Verification**: temporarily removed the two new effects (a real, targeted revert) and reran -- failed exactly as predicted; restored and reran clean. Full `EntityPanel.test.ts` (177/177) passes, confirming no regression to round 751's own `fieldFilters` test or any other group-by/filter test. Only `apps/web` changed this round, so its own full suite ran: 1104/1104 pass, no flakes. `tsc -b` clean.

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. ### Round 782: uploading a file with a Hebrew/non-ASCII filename corrupted it into permanent mojibake everywhere it's displayed

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey moved to the file-upload path, a different corner of the app from the per-entity UI live-refine staleness bugs rounds 777-781 focused on.

**The gap**: multer (via busboy, installed version 1.6.0) decodes a multipart part's `Content-Disposition: filename="..."` header using a strict byte-for-byte Latin-1 mapping (`latin1Slice` plus busboy's default `nullDecoder`) unless a `defParamCharset` is explicitly configured on the middleware -- which this app's own `createUploadMiddleware` (`apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts`) never does. Every real browser (Chrome/Firefox/Safari), and Node's own native `fetch`/`FormData`/`File` implementation (confirmed empirically with a live script, not assumed), sends a non-ASCII filename as its raw UTF-8 bytes directly in that header -- not RFC 5987 `filename*=UTF-8''...` percent-encoding, and not real Latin-1. The result: uploading a file named e.g. "קורות חיים.pdf" to a `file`-type field -- an entirely ordinary action for this app's primary Hebrew-speaking user base -- corrupted `file.originalname` into mojibake, each UTF-8 byte individually mis-mapped to its own Latin-1 code point. That corrupted string then became the file field's permanent, displayed `name`: the record table cell, CSV/backup export, WhatsApp/webhook automation message templates that reference the field, and Global Search all show the garbled text forever, with no way for the user to fix it short of re-uploading under an ASCII-only filename.

**Why this is not deliberate**: nothing in `createUploadMiddleware` or the upload route suggests charset handling was ever considered; the corruption happens silently inside multer/busboy's own default decoding path, several layers below this app's own code, with no error surfaced anywhere.

**The fix**: `decodeMojibakeFilename()` re-interprets the Latin-1 code points as UTF-8 bytes -- the exact inverse of the mis-decoding -- gated by two guards, both necessary: (1) every character in the string must be in the Latin-1 range (U+0000-U+00FF). busboy's own `filename*=UTF-8''...` RFC 5987 extended syntax is *already* correctly charset-decoded independent of `defParamCharset` (confirmed by reading busboy's own `parseDispositionParams` source directly) -- so a filename that arrived via that path is already genuine Unicode text and always has at least one character outside the Latin-1 range; re-decoding it a second time would corrupt it. (2) the re-decode result must not introduce the U+FFFD replacement character, which signals the original bytes were never valid UTF-8 to begin with -- e.g. a genuine single-byte Latin-1 accented filename ("café.pdf") sent by some older, non-UTF-8 client -- in which case the original string is already correct and must be returned unchanged rather than further corrupted. Wired into the upload route's JSON response (`name: decodeMojibakeFilename(file.originalname)`).

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- the exported standalone app has no file-upload endpoint of its own at all.

**The tests**: added 4 new unit tests for `decodeMojibakeFilename` directly in `projects.test.ts` (plain ASCII filename passes through unchanged; a simulated mojibake string round-trips back to the real Hebrew text; already-correct Unicode Hebrew text -- genuinely outside the Latin-1 range, not merely accented -- is never re-decoded a second time; a genuine single-byte Latin-1 name is left alone because re-decoding it as UTF-8 would be invalid) plus one new integration test in `app.test.ts` that uploads a real file via multipart `FormData` with a Hebrew filename through the actual HTTP route and asserts the returned `file.name` is the exact original text, not mojibake.

**Verification**: reverted the fix end-to-end (upload route back to raw `file.originalname`) and reran the integration test -- failed with the exact predicted mojibake string; restored and reran clean. Independently removed each guard in the unit-test function in turn: removing the U+FFFD guard reproduced the predicted failure on the genuine-Latin1-name test exactly as expected; removing the Latin-1-range guard did not independently fail any current test, because `Buffer.from(str, "latin1")`'s truncation of out-of-range UTF-16 code units on this file's Hebrew fixture happens to also produce invalid UTF-8 that the other guard already catches -- documented honestly rather than manufacturing an artificial fixture to force that line to look independently required; the range guard stays in place as correct defense-in-depth against a hypothetical input where truncation could coincidentally produce valid-but-wrong UTF-8 with no U+FFFD. Only `apps/api` changed this round, so its own full suite ran: 552/553 pass, the sole failure being the already-documented pre-existing `codegen.test.ts` process-exit hang flake (location `:1:1`, SIGKILL), unrelated to this change. `npm run build` (esbuild bundle) clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed.

### Round 783: signup, login, and forgot-password had no limit at all on how many times they could be called

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey moved to a different corner of the app than recent rounds: the auth layer's own abuse surface, rather than per-entity UI live-refine staleness or file uploads.

**The gap**: nothing in `apps/api` enforced any limit on how many times `POST /auth/signup`, `POST /auth/login`, or `POST /auth/forgot-password` could be called (confirmed by reading `app.ts`'s full middleware chain and grepping the whole `apps/api/src` tree for any rate-limiting mechanism -- there was none). `routes/auth.ts` already invested real, documented effort defending `/auth/login` against a timing side-channel (`dummyPasswordHashPromise`) and account enumeration (deliberately generic responses) -- but `verifyPassword`'s scrypt cost is attacker-side CPU, not a server-enforced limit, so an unbounded loop could brute-force a password at whatever rate the attacker's own hardware allows. The same absence let `/auth/signup` be hit in a loop to mass-create accounts/rows, and let `/auth/forgot-password` be hit in a loop against a known victim email to send that victim a real reset email on every single call with no throttle at all -- email-bombing their inbox and burning this deployment's Resend quota -- and, since a fresh password-reset or login-code request always invalidates whichever one came before it for the same account (`deletePasswordResetTokensForUser`/`deleteLoginCodesForUser`, both pre-existing and deliberate for their own stated reasons), also usable to repeatedly invalidate a legitimate pending code or reset link out from under a user mid-login.

**Why this is not deliberate**: the surrounding code in this exact file shows clear, deliberate security investment elsewhere (the timing-side-channel fix, the enumeration-safe generic responses) -- there's no sign request-rate was ever considered at all, just a gap several layers above where that other, more subtle work already happened.

**The fix**: a small in-memory fixed-window rate limiter (`auth/rateLimit.ts`), applied to all three routes. Deliberately no background `setInterval` sweep to bound the tracked-keys map's memory -- `automations.ts`'s own `startScheduledAutomationsLoop` doc comment already documents exactly why a timer started from inside `createApp()`/`createAuthRouter()` would leak one per test across the hundreds of app instances `app.test.ts`'s `withServer` helper creates; expired buckets are instead swept lazily, piggybacking on whichever request happens to find the map larger than a bounded size, so there's no timer to leak at all. Each `createAuthRouter()` call gets its own fresh limiter instances -- the same per-call-creation convention `app.ts`'s own `activePipelines` Set already follows -- so no rate-limit state leaks between unrelated app instances or tests. `signup` and `login` are keyed by IP (20 and 30 per 15 minutes respectively) -- the realistic attack there is one machine iterating quickly. `forgot-password` is keyed by the *target* email, not IP (5 per 15 minutes) -- the actual harm (spamming one inbox) doesn't depend on which IP the request comes from, and this also directly caps the login-code/reset-token-invalidation side effect described above. A 429 uses the existing `HttpError`/`RATE_LIMITED` convention.

**i18n**: added `error.RATE_LIMITED` in both Hebrew and English -- caught automatically by `i18n/language.test.ts`'s existing "every HttpError code the API can send has a translation" source-scanning test, which would otherwise have let this one new code silently fall back to raw English text for this app's primary Hebrew-speaking user base.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- the exported standalone app has no auth system of its own at all.

**The tests**: 3 new unit tests for `createRateLimiter` directly (blocks the request that exceeds `max`; tracks separate keys independently -- one key's exhaustion never affects another; resets a key's count once its window fully elapses, using an injected `Date.now`) plus 3 new integration tests that drive the real routes past their limits end-to-end: signup's 21st distinct-email attempt from one IP is blocked with 429 while the first 20 still succeed normally; login's 31st attempt is blocked while the first 30 still get their normal (non-429) response; a 6th `forgot-password` request for the same victim email is blocked while a request for a completely different target email is unaffected.

**Verification**: temporarily removed the middleware wiring on all three routes (a real, targeted revert) and reran -- all 3 new integration tests failed exactly as predicted (expected 429, got the normal unblocked status); restored and reran clean. Specifically re-ran the pre-existing `/auth/login` timing-side-channel test (13 login calls in a single test) and the login-code-invalidation test (3 logins in a single test) to confirm the chosen limits (30/15min, comfortably above both call counts) don't collide with legitimate existing test traffic -- they didn't. Full `apps/api` suite: 558/559 pass, the sole failure being the already-documented pre-existing `codegen.test.ts` process-exit hang flake (location `:1:1`, SIGKILL), unrelated to this change. `apps/web`: `tsc -b` clean; `i18n/language.test.ts` 20/20, including the HttpError-code-translation-coverage scan.

**Status**: shipped and pushed.

### Round 784: Time Machine's diff and "Current" check silently ignored a field's required flag

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey moved to the Time Machine (checkpoint history) feature, a different corner of the app from the auth layer rounds 782-783 focused on.

**The gap**: `checkpointDiff.ts`'s `fieldSignature()` -- the "shape" two same-named fields are compared by, used by both `computeCheckpointDiff` (the diff list shown per checkpoint) and `isCheckpointCurrent` (the "Current" chip) -- only ever compared `type`, `relationTo`, and `enumValues`. It deliberately (and correctly) never compares `label`, since a label rename is cosmetic, with its own doc comment saying exactly that. But it also silently never compared `required`, with no comment acknowledging the omission at all -- even though `required` is a genuine behavioral property, not cosmetic: `repository.ts`'s `coerceValue` rejects a missing value once a field is required. `apps/api/src/pipeline.ts`'s own `computeImpact` already treats exactly this change (a field becoming required) as a tracked "tightened" structural change worth its own build-time warning -- proving the team already considers this a real, reportable change; the independently-written Time Machine diff logic in a completely different file just never got the same treatment.

**Why this is not deliberate**: the one existing test that touched this exact combination (`"computeCheckpointDiff never flags a field as changed just because its label or required-ness differs"`) actually asserted the bug as intended behavior -- but `fieldSignature`'s own doc comment only ever explained the label omission, never the required one, and a parallel, already-fixed property in a sibling file (`pipeline.ts`'s `tightenedFieldNames`) treats the identical flag as worth tracking.

**Concrete failure scenario**: build a project with `Customer.email` optional, then refine it to make `email` required (same field name, same type). Opening History/Time Machine: the original checkpoint still gets the "Current" chip (`isCheckpointCurrent` wrongly returns `true`), and the diff view reports zero changes for that field (`computeCheckpointDiff`'s `changedFieldNames` is empty) -- even though restoring that checkpoint would genuinely make the field optional again, a real difference from the live app.

**The fix**: folded `required` into `fieldSignature`'s string, the same symmetric treatment `type`/`enum`/`relation` already get -- flagged as changed in *either* direction (loosened or tightened), not just the one-directional "tightening" `pipeline.ts`'s own narrower build-time-warning feature cares about.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- the exported standalone app has no Time Machine/checkpoint feature of its own at all.

**The tests**: the one existing test that encoded the bug as intended behavior was split into two -- a label-only test (kept, still correctly expecting no change) and a new required-only test (now correctly expecting `changedFieldNames` to report it). Added a parallel new `isCheckpointCurrent` test for the identical gap (same name/type, only the required flag differs -> not current).

**Verification**: reverted `fieldSignature`'s new required segment and reran -- both new tests failed exactly as predicted (a `deepEqual` mismatch on `changedFieldNames`; `true !== false` on `isCheckpointCurrent`); restored and reran clean. Full `checkpointDiff.test.ts`: 38/38 pass. Only `apps/web` changed this round, so its own full suite ran: 1107/1107 pass, no flakes. `tsc -b` clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed.

### Round 785: a customer's incoming WhatsApp photo, voice note, or document was silently dropped -- no row, no log entry, nothing

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey moved to WhatsApp incoming-message handling, a different corner of the app from the Time Machine checkpoint logic round 784 focused on.

**The gap**: `handleIncomingMessages` (`apps/api/src/whatsappWeb.ts`) only ever read `msg.message?.conversation` and `msg.message?.extendedTextMessage?.text`, then `continue`d -- no row inserted at all -- whenever both were empty. Baileys shapes a photo/video/voice-note/document/sticker completely differently from a plain text message: none of those populate `conversation`/`extendedTextMessage`, only a type-specific key (`imageMessage`/`videoMessage`/`audioMessage`/`documentMessage`/`stickerMessage`), each with its own optional `caption` (audio and stickers have none at all -- WhatsApp itself doesn't support a caption on either). None of those keys were ever read anywhere in this file, confirmed by grepping the whole repo for them.

**Why this is not deliberate**: there's no comment anywhere suggesting non-text messages were ever considered and intentionally excluded -- the plain text-only lookup is just an incomplete read of Baileys' real, much richer message shape.

**Concrete failure scenario**: a customer texts a connected WhatsApp number a photo of a damaged product, or a voice note placing an order, with no caption. The message simply never appeared anywhere -- no row in `whatsapp_messages`, nothing in the WhatsApp log UI, no indication to the business owner that a message had even arrived. This is a materially common case for this feature's own target users (couriers, small retail, service businesses), not an edge case.

**The fix**: `describeIncomingMessage()` recognizes the five common media kinds and builds a bracketed, plain-English placeholder (`"[Photo]"`, `"[Video]"`, `"[Voice note]"`/`"[Audio]"` depending on the `ptt` flag, `"[Document: <filename>]"`, `"[Sticker]"`), appending the real caption when the kind has one and it's non-empty -- matching this file's own `QR_EXPIRED_MESSAGE`/`CONNECTION_LOST_MESSAGE` convention of plain English for backend-origin text, since this isn't a UI-chrome string with an error code the client can translate. A row is now always inserted for these kinds, so the business owner at least sees that something arrived and what kind, even though the actual photo/voice note/document content isn't retrievable from here. Deliberately scoped to just these five verified shapes -- a genuinely unrecognized message (a contact card, location pin, poll, etc.) still returns `null` and is skipped exactly as before, rather than guessing at an unverified shape.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- the exported standalone app has no WhatsApp integration of its own at all.

**The tests**: one new test drives all five media kinds (including both with and without a caption/fileName, and both `ptt` true/false for audio) through the real `emitMessagesUpsert` path and asserts each produced row has the exact expected placeholder body (ordering matches `listWhatsAppMessages`' own documented newest-first order -- caught and fixed a first-draft mistake in the test itself, which initially asserted insertion order rather than the real newest-first query order). A second new test confirms a genuinely unrecognized message shape is still skipped, preserving the existing "no body -> no row" behavior for everything else.

**Verification**: reverted `describeIncomingMessage`'s call site back to the old plain-text-only lookup and reran -- the new media test failed exactly as predicted (0 rows inserted instead of 7); restored and reran clean. Full `whatsappWeb.test.ts`: 25/25. Only `apps/api` changed this round, so its own full suite ran: 560/561 pass; the sole failure is the already-documented pre-existing `codegen.test.ts` process-exit hang flake (location `:1:1`, SIGKILL), unrelated to this change. `npm run build` (esbuild bundle) clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed.

### Round 786: WhatsApp automations could only ever mention a file's name -- the actual uploaded file was never attached to the outgoing message

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey moved to outgoing WhatsApp automation behavior -- a different, previously-unexamined layer from the incoming-media-logging fix round 785 just shipped.

**The gap**: `WhatsAppWebManager.sendMessage` (`apps/api/src/whatsappWeb.ts`) only ever called `session.sock.sendMessage(jid, { text: body })` -- there was no code path anywhere for sending an actual attachment, even though Baileys (the underlying library) supports one. `automations.ts`'s `interpolateTemplate` deliberately resolves a `"file"`-type field's `{{fieldName}}` placeholder down to just its bare filename as plain text (`fileFieldDisplayName`'s own doc comment explains why that's correct for the text) -- but the real uploaded file itself was never actually sent anywhere, through any path.

**Why this is not deliberate**: the create-rule UI's own hint explicitly invites referencing *any* field by name in a message template, with no caveat that a file field behaves any differently from a text field beyond how it's displayed -- there's no comment or design note anywhere suggesting attachments were ever considered and ruled out.

**Concrete failure scenario**: an automation rule "when status=Delivered, WhatsApp the customer their invoice" with a template like "here's your invoice: `{{invoice}}`" only ever sent the customer a text message naming a file ("invoice-203.pdf") they never actually received.

**The fix**: `WhatsAppSocket.sendMessage`'s content type now also accepts a document shape (`{ document: Buffer, mimetype, fileName, caption }`). `WhatsAppWebManager.sendMessage` takes a new optional `WhatsAppAttachment` (`filePath`/`fileName`/`mimeType`) and, when given one, reads the file from disk and sends it as a document with the message text as its caption -- falling back to a plain text send (not a reported failure) if the file can no longer be read, since the referenced upload may have been deleted or replaced since the rule last ran. `automations.ts`'s new `findTemplateFileAttachment` mirrors `routes/projects.ts`'s own `deleteUploadedFile` -- the only other place that turns a file field's stored `{url, name, size, mimeType}` descriptor back into a real path on disk (`uploadsDir/projectId/entityName/<storedFilename>`). Scoped to the FIRST file field referenced in the template, in placeholder order -- WhatsApp only supports one attachment per message. `fireRule` resolves this and passes it through to `sendMessage`; `runAutomationsForRecordChange` gained a new `uploadsDir` parameter to thread it down from `routes/projects.ts`'s two call sites (POST and PATCH on a record), which already have `uploadsDir` in scope. `fireScheduledRule` and the webhook action path are both unaffected -- a schedule rule has no triggering record (so no file field could ever resolve), and a webhook payload already carries the file's raw `{url,...}` descriptor, so a webhook consumer can already fetch it themselves.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- the exported standalone app has no WhatsApp integration or automations engine of its own at all.

**Deliberately NOT done this round** (separate, larger pieces of the same underlying gap, left as noted future work rather than guessed at): the manual "send test message" route/UI has no file picker either; and image/video mimetypes are always sent as a generic "document" rather than Baileys' richer image/video content types with an inline chat preview.

**The tests**: `findTemplateFileAttachment` gets 2 new direct unit tests (resolves the first file field referenced; returns `null` when no file field is referenced, the referenced field has no value, or the referenced field isn't a `'file'` type at all). A new integration test drives `runAutomationsForRecordChange` end-to-end with a real file on disk under a real temp uploads directory and asserts the fake WhatsApp manager receives the correct attachment alongside the still-unchanged text. `whatsappWeb.ts` gets 2 new tests: `sendMessage` reads a real file and sends it as a document with the right mimetype/fileName/caption, and gracefully falls back to a plain text send when the attachment's file is missing from disk.

**Verification**: reverted `fireRule`'s attachment resolution (passing no attachment to `sendMessage`) and reran -- the new `automations.test.ts` attachment test failed exactly as predicted (attachment `undefined` instead of resolved); restored and reran clean. Separately reverted `whatsappWeb.ts`'s own attachment-handling (forcing the read buffer to always be `null`) and reran -- the new `whatsappWeb.test.ts` attachment test failed exactly as predicted (sent as plain text instead of a document); restored and reran clean. Full `whatsappWeb.test.ts`: 27/27. `automations.test.ts`: 42/42. Only `apps/api` changed this round, so its own full suite ran: 565/566 pass; the sole failure is the already-documented pre-existing `codegen.test.ts` process-exit hang flake (location `:1:1`, SIGKILL), unrelated to this change. `npm run build` (esbuild bundle) clean.

### Round 787: restoring a Time Machine checkpoint never warned about a re-tightened field or a vanishing entity, the same hazard /build and /refine already flag

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey moved to checkpoint-restore's own warning parity with /build and /refine -- a different layer from the outgoing WhatsApp attachment work round 786 just shipped.

**The gap**: `pipeline.ts`'s `computeImpact`/`architectEvent` is the only place that compares a previous spec against a next one for (a) entities removed from the spec, (b) fields removed from a surviving entity, and (c) fields "tightened" (becoming required where they weren't, or an enum losing a value) -- each surfaced as a "Warning: ..." clause in the Architect's own build/refine message. This function was module-private and only ever called from `runBuildPipeline`, i.e. only reachable via `POST /build` and `POST /refine`. The checkpoint-restore route (`POST /projects/:id/checkpoints/:checkpointId/restore`) already calls `diffAndMigrate(db, project.id, project.spec, checkpoint.spec)` -- the exact same previousSpec/nextSpec shape `computeImpact` expects -- but never produced this warning class at all, confirmed by reading both functions directly and grepping `pipeline.ts`'s own export list.

**Why this is not deliberate**: nothing in the restore route's own code or comments ever addresses this specific hazard class -- its existing comments only discuss the schema-level `diffAndMigrate` hazards (`type_changed`/`relation_*`/`automation_rule_disabled`, via `describeMigrationHazards`), a different, narrower function with no concept of "field removed," "entity removed," or "field tightened" at all.

**Why this matters**: restoring to an older checkpoint is not a safe, monotonically-looser operation just because the underlying data migration is additive-only. Each build/refine regenerates the whole spec fresh (AI or heuristic), so an earlier checkpoint can easily be STRICTER than the current spec on some field, or can simply predate an entity/field the user has been actively using with real data in it. Concretely: build a project with `Customer.email` required; refine relaxes it to optional (correctly, no warning -- loosening is never flagged); several customer records get created with no email, now legal; restoring to the original checkpoint silently re-enables the `required` constraint with zero notice, the identical hazard /refine already warns about via `tightenedFieldNames`. Separately: if a later refine added a whole new entity with real records, restoring to a checkpoint that predates it makes that entity (and its data) vanish from every tab with no "N entities are no longer in the spec" warning either.

**The fix**: `computeImpact` is now exported, and its three "Warning: ..." clauses are extracted into a new exported `describeImpactHazards()`, reused by `architectEvent` itself (a pure refactor, verified behavior-identical via the full existing `pipeline.test.ts` suite passing unchanged) and now also called from the restore route, appended to the existing `migrationWarning` string alongside `describeMigrationHazards`' own "Note: ..." clauses.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- the exported standalone app has no Time Machine/checkpoint feature of its own at all.

**The tests**: 2 new direct unit tests for `describeImpactHazards` (reports a removed entity, a removed field, and a tightened field all at once; returns an empty string for identical specs or a purely additive change -- a new optional field is never a hazard). 2 new integration tests drive the real restore route end-to-end via the DB layer (the same determinism convention this file's existing `migrationWarning` tests already use, engineering the "later refine" step directly rather than depending on what a real spec generator happens to produce): one engineers a field relaxed then restored back to required, the other an entity added then restored back out of existence -- both assert the expected "Warning: ..." text comes back in `migrationWarning`.

**Verification**: reverted the restore route's new `describeImpactHazards` call and reran -- both new integration tests failed exactly as predicted (no `migrationWarning` present); restored and reran clean. Full `app.test.ts`: 229/229. `pipeline.test.ts`: 30/30, confirming the `architectEvent` refactor produces byte-identical messages to before. Only `apps/api` changed this round, so its own full suite ran: 569/570 pass; the sole failure is the already-documented pre-existing `codegen.test.ts` process-exit hang flake (location `:1:1`, SIGKILL), unrelated to this change. `npm run build` (esbuild bundle) clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed.

### Round 788: a webhook automation's JSON payload sent a file field as a doubly-encoded, unusable string with a relative URL

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey moved to the webhook action type -- a sibling of the WhatsApp automation path rounds 786-787 focused on, but a different delivery mechanism.

**The gap**: `fireWebhookAction`'s JSON payload (`apps/api/src/automations.ts`) embedded `record` completely untouched -- unlike `message`, which `interpolateTemplate` carefully special-cases a `"file"`-type field for (`fileFieldDisplayName`, just the filename, for exactly this reason). A file field's stored value is itself a JSON-encoded `{url, name, size, mimeType}` descriptor string (`repository.ts` never special-cases `"file"` at the storage layer -- confirmed by grepping it directly). `JSON.stringify`-ing the whole payload then embeds that descriptor as a doubly-escaped JSON *string* nested inside the outer JSON body (e.g. `"pdf": "{\"url\":...}"`), not a usable nested object -- and even parsed, `url` is this server's own relative path (`"/api/uploads/..."`), meaningless to the exact external consumer the create-rule UI explicitly advertises ("works with Zapier, Slack, Make, or any other system"): none of those services auto-parse a JSON string buried inside a JSON value, and none of them know this server's own origin to resolve a relative path against even if they did.

**Why this is not deliberate**: every other export/render surface in this codebase that touches a file field's value (CSV export, ICS export, `interpolateTemplate`, the backup ZIP) carries an explicit file-type branch to avoid exactly this class of leak -- the webhook payload is the one surface that never got the same treatment.

**Concrete failure scenario**: an Invoice entity with a `pdf: file` field and a `record_created` rule configured to call a Zapier webhook -- every fired event's `record.pdf` arrived as opaque escaped text, silently breaking the one piece of information (the actual file) most users configuring this would want to act on downstream.

**The fix**: `automations.ts`'s new `resolveFileFieldsForWebhook` parses every file field's descriptor and rewrites its `url` to a real, fully-qualified URL (via `new URL(relativeUrl, baseUrl)`), leaving every other field untouched; a value that isn't a real file descriptor at all (empty, malformed) is left exactly as-is, the same graceful degradation `fileFieldDisplayName` already uses. Returns a plain `Record<string, unknown>`, not `EntityRecord` -- that type is `string | number | boolean | null` only, and a resolved descriptor is a nested object, so this is deliberately a different, wider shape used only for this one JSON payload, never fed back into any `EntityRecord`-typed code path. `fireWebhookAction`, `fireRule`, and `runAutomationsForRecordChange` all gained a new `baseUrl` parameter (`null` when there's no record/entity at all -- `fireScheduledRule`'s own webhook path, which could never reference a file field in the first place) threaded down from `routes/projects.ts`'s two `runAutomationsForRecordChange` call sites, built the same way `/auth/forgot-password`'s own reset-link already is: `` `${req.protocol}://${req.get("host")}` ``.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- the exported standalone app has no automations engine of its own at all.

**The tests**: a new integration test drives `runAutomationsForRecordChange` through a webhook rule with a real file field and asserts the fired payload's `record.pdf` is now a genuine nested object with a fully-qualified URL, while every other field (and the text message itself) is unaffected. A new direct unit test for `resolveFileFieldsForWebhook` confirms non-file fields and empty/malformed file values are left exactly as-is.

**Verification**: reverted `fireWebhookAction`'s own file-field resolution (passing the raw record straight through) and reran -- the new integration test failed exactly as predicted (the raw doubly-encoded JSON string instead of a resolved object); restored and reran clean. Full `automations.test.ts`: 44/44. `app.test.ts`: 229/229, confirming the `routes/projects.ts` signature changes broke nothing. Only `apps/api` changed this round, so its own full suite ran: 571/572 pass; the sole failure is the already-documented pre-existing `codegen.test.ts` process-exit hang flake (location `:1:1`, SIGKILL), unrelated to this change. `npm run build` (esbuild bundle) clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed.

### Round 789: the webhook SSRF guard's IPv4-mapped-IPv6 unwrapping missed the RFC 6052 NAT64 encoding of the same blocked-IP bypass

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey went back to the webhook SSRF guard -- not the already-reviewed-and-accepted DNS-rebinding gap, but a different, static-literal encoding gap in the existing IPv4-mapped-address unwrapping this exact file already has a fix for under one specific prefix.

**The gap**: `extractIPv4MappedAddress` (`apps/api/src/automations.ts`) already unwraps the `"::ffff:"` IPv4-mapped-IPv6 encoding (e.g. `"[::ffff:169.254.169.254]"`) back to its embedded IPv4 address, specifically so `BLOCKED_IPV4_HOSTNAME_PATTERNS` can still catch a blocked target hiding behind that encoding -- but its regex only ever matched that one prefix. RFC 6052's well-known NAT64 prefix (`"64:ff9b::"`) embeds an IPv4 address inside an IPv6 literal the exact same way, used by any network that actually performs NAT64/DNS64 translation (common on IPv6-mostly networks and some cloud/container egress setups). Confirmed empirically (`node -e "console.log(new URL('http://[64:ff9b::169.254.169.254]/').hostname)"`) that Node's own URL parser canonicalizes that literal to `"[64:ff9b::a9fe:a9fe]"` -- the identical hex-pair shape `"::ffff:"` already produces, just under a prefix the original regex never recognized at all, so it fell through to `BLOCKED_OTHER_HOSTNAME_PATTERNS` (none of which know about this prefix either) and `isAllowedWebhookUrl` wrongly returned `true` for a webhook URL literally addressing the AWS/GCP instance-metadata IP.

**Why this is not deliberate**: this file's own extensive comment history already treats "a blocked IP hiding behind a different IPv6 encoding" as a recognized, actively-defended-against hazard class (the exact reasoning behind `extractIPv4MappedAddress` existing at all) -- it just covered one of the two real-world encodings of that class, not both.

**The fix**: `extractIPv4MappedAddress`'s regex now matches either prefix (`"::ffff:"` or `"64:ff9b::"`) before extracting the embedded IPv4 address -- the rest of the unwrapping/validation logic is unchanged, since both prefixes produce the identical embedded-address shape.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- the exported standalone app has no automations engine of its own at all.

**The tests**: a new test mirrors the existing `"::ffff:"` IPv4-mapped-literal test exactly, for the NAT64 prefix instead -- confirms the cloud instance-metadata IP, loopback (dotted and hex form), and a private `10.x` address wrapped with `"64:ff9b::"` are all still blocked, while a genuinely public IPv4 address wrapped the same way is still allowed.

**Verification**: reverted the regex back to `"::ffff:"`-only and reran -- the new test failed exactly as predicted (the blocked instance-metadata IP wrongly allowed through); restored and reran clean. Full `automations.test.ts`: 45/45. Only `apps/api` changed this round, so its own full suite ran: 572/573 pass; the sole failure is the already-documented pre-existing `codegen.test.ts` process-exit hang flake (location `:1:1`, SIGKILL), unrelated to this change. `npm run build` (esbuild bundle) clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed.

### Round 790: Global Search's "Show all" left a stale relation-label cache behind for every OTHER entity's own "Show all"

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey moved to Global Search internals -- a different corner of the app from the webhook/automations work rounds 788-789 focused on.

**The gap**: `handleShowAll` (`apps/web/src/GlobalSearchPanel.tsx`) re-fetches one entity's own records fresh -- specifically to catch data that changed while the panel stayed open (a collaborator's edit, a WhatsApp-matched write), per its own existing doc comment from round 556 -- but never wrote that fresh data back into `lastRecordsByEntityRef`, the shared cache every entity's relation-field matching reads from. `matchesSearch` resolves a relation field's value to its target record's display label via this exact ref, to determine whether a record counts as matching the search query at all.

**Why this is not deliberate**: `handleShowAll`'s own doc comment already explicitly explains the purpose of its fresh re-fetch (catching exactly this kind of external change) -- it just never extended that same freshness to the ONE shared cache other entities depend on for resolving a relation pointing at the entity being refreshed.

**Concrete failure scenario**: search "Dana" matches a Courier directly and, via a relation, every Order whose `courierId` points at that courier. Click "Show all" on Courier -- its own count correctly updates once renamed away from "Dana" elsewhere (a collaborator, another tab) -- but clicking "Show all" on Order afterward still resolves `courierId`'s display label from the ORIGINAL search's now-stale snapshot, not the fresh data Courier's own "Show all" just fetched (and is already sitting in memory from that very request): Order's "Show all" wrongly keeps counting an order whose courier no longer matches the query at all.

**The fix**: `handleShowAll` now writes `{ ...lastRecordsByEntityRef.current, [entityName]: records }` into the ref immediately after its own fresh fetch, before calling `searchEntityRecords` -- so any other entity's relation pointing at this one (and this entity's own relation fields, if any) resolve against the data this exact request just pulled, not whatever the original search last saw.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed needed and applied -- the exported standalone app's `GlobalSearch.jsx` is a deliberate duplicate of `handleShowAll` with the identical gap, fixed with the identical one-line write-back.

A new `codegen.test.ts` test runs the real generated `handleShowAll` directly (pre-seeded with a stale snapshot) and confirms it overwrites `lastRecordsByEntityRef` with its own fresh fetch.

**Verification**: the live DOM test's first draft actually passed even against the UNFIXED code -- caught via tracing the real cache contents and the real computed sample size at each step: waiting for the "Show all" button to disappear isn't on its own a correct discriminating signal, since it disappears either way (`totalMatches` always gets set to whatever was just computed, buggy or not). Corrected the test to assert the final hit count directly instead. With that correction, reverting the fix made the corrected test fail exactly as predicted (6 matches instead of 5); restored and reran clean. Same revert-and-confirm cycle for the `codegen.ts` port. ### Round 792: single-record PATCH/DELETE had no protection against a lost-response retry

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey moved to the request-retry/idempotency machinery itself (`docs/wakeRetry-idempotency-design.md`, round 470) -- specifically, which of the mutating routes actually use it.

**The gap**: every other mutating route in `apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts` (record create, bulk import, etc.) wraps its handler in `withIdempotency`, but the two single-record routes -- `PATCH` and `DELETE /projects/:id/entities/:entityName/:recordId` -- never did. A response lost in transit after the mutation already committed (dropped connection, client timeout -- exactly the case `fetchWithWakeRetry` on the frontend exists to retry) left a retry free to run the underlying mutation a second time with no guard at all.

**Why this is not deliberate**: `withIdempotency` already exists specifically for this purpose and is already wired into every comparable route; these two were simply missed when it was introduced.

**Concrete failure scenario, DELETE**: a client's own DELETE succeeds server-side, but the response never arrives; `fetchWithWakeRetry` resends it. The retry hits `deleteRecord` against an already-deleted row, which throws `NotFoundError` -- the retry the client sent specifically to recover from a lost response instead came back 404 for a request that had, in fact, already succeeded.

**Concrete failure scenario, PATCH**: subtler, since re-sending the exact same body twice is harmless on its own -- `updateRecord` just rewrites the same value back, so a retry that merely repeats the original request lands on the same final state whether or not anything guards it. The real, observable harm needs a genuinely different edit landing in between the lost response and the retry: a collaborator's own PATCH (using no idempotency key of its own, racing in while the original caller's response never arrived) changes the same field to a newer value; the original caller's retry, still carrying its own stale body, then clobbers that collaborator's newer edit back down to the old value.

**The fix**: both routes now wrap their handlers in `withIdempotency`, matching the existing pattern. DELETE's callback returns `{status: 204, body: null}` (`JSON.stringify(null)` is a valid cached-response string; `JSON.stringify(undefined)` is not, which is why `null` rather than `undefined` here). PATCH's callback moves `updateRecord`, the orphaned-file cleanup, and the automation trigger all inside the guarded callback, so none of them re-run on a replayed retry. `apps/web/src/api.ts`'s `updateRecord`/`deleteRecord` now each send a fresh `x-idempotency-key` per call, so the browser's own `fetchWithWakeRetry` retry path actually benefits from this.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- the exported standalone app has no idempotency mechanism of any kind for any route.

**The tests**: DELETE -- retried with the same key after the first attempt already finished replays the cached 204 instead of 404ing. PATCH went through two invalid designs before landing on one that actually discriminates: the first draft asserted the retry's response and final record state matched the first attempt exactly, but that passed even with the fix reverted, since an identical-body retry is naturally idempotent at the storage layer regardless of any guard. The second draft tried proving the point via a `field_equals` automation rule's run count, reasoning a duplicate execution would double-fire it -- that also passed with the fix reverted, because `computeChangedFields` diffs the retry's own fresh before/after snapshot, which is already stable by the time an identical-payload retry runs, so the trigger naturally doesn't match a second time independent of any guard. The version that actually works interleaves a collaborator's own, separately-keyed PATCH between the first attempt and the retry, and asserts the collaborator's edit survives the retry rather than being clobbered back to the retry's own stale body.

**Verification**: both new tests verified via revert/restore. DELETE: fails with "404 !== 204" when the fix is reverted, passes when restored. PATCH: fails with the collaborator's edit clobbered (`"Dana Cohen"` instead of `"Dana Smith"`) when the fix is reverted, passes when restored. Only `apps/api` changed this round, so its own full suite ran: 574/575 pass; the sole failure is the already-documented pre-existing `codegen.test.ts` process-exit hang flake (location `:1:1`, SIGKILL), stopping at the identical subtest it has in every round's log since 787 -- confirmed unrelated to this change.

**Status**: shipped and pushed.

### Round 793: `pickDisplayField`'s name-hint step never excluded relation/file fields

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey moved to the "which field represents a record by name" logic itself -- a foundational helper read from dozens of call sites across both workspaces, not touched by any of the rounds immediately before it.

**The gap**: `pickDisplayField` (duplicated identically in `apps/api/src/displayField.ts`, `apps/web/src/entityFormatting.ts`, and `apps/api/src/codegen.ts`) picks the field that best represents a record as a short human label: prefer a field named "name"/"title", then the first text field, then the first non-relation/non-file field, then whatever's left. The last two steps explicitly exclude `relation` and `file` fields -- documented reasoning going back to rounds 741/749: without it, `recordDisplayLabel` would `String()` a relation's raw foreign-key id or a file's raw JSON upload descriptor as the record's own label. The very first step never got that same treatment -- it matched purely on `field.name.toLowerCase()` against `["name", "title"]`, with no check on `field.type` at all.

**Why this is not deliberate**: every other "match by field-name hint" helper in this codebase follows the opposite, safer order -- filter candidates by type first, then apply the name hint within that already-safe pool (`findBoardField`, the date-field picker). `pickDisplayField` was the one exception, even though its own later steps already reason carefully, in their own doc comments, about this exact hazard class -- just never extended that reasoning one step earlier.

**Concrete failure scenario**: `Employee { title: relation->JobTitle, department: text }` -- a normalized job-title lookup, a perfectly plausible real-world schema. `pickDisplayField` returns the `title` relation field purely because of its name, before the type-aware fallback steps ever run. `recordDisplayLabel` then prints the raw foreign-key integer (e.g. `"7"`, itself the id of some *JobTitle* row, not the Employee's own id) as the employee's label everywhere one is shown by name: relation picker cells/dropdowns elsewhere in the app, CSV import's relation-cell matching (silently breaks re-importing a CSV exported with real names, or worse, can mismatch against a JobTitle id that happens to equal the typed text), Business Twin's "most-linked record" narrative sentence, and WhatsApp automation template interpolation (a real recipient gets a message naming an employee by a bare digit). The identical hazard applies to a file field named "name" (e.g. `Document { name: file }`), where the raw JSON upload descriptor gets printed instead.

**The fix**: the name-hint step's `find()` predicate now also requires `f.type !== "relation" && f.type !== "file"`, mirroring the existing `firstDisplayable` step exactly, in all three copies.

**codegen.ts parity**: needed and applied -- all three copies were byte-for-byte identical in this function before the fix.

**The tests**: one new regression test per copy (a relation field literally named "title" plus a file field literally named "name", each paired with a plain text field that should win instead). `codegen.test.ts`'s version drives the real generated function via `new Function()`, matching that file's existing convention for this helper.

**Verification**: each new test verified independently via revert/restore -- reverting the type check in each file's own copy made its own new test fail exactly as predicted (the relation/file field won by name instead of the later text field); restoring made it pass. Both workspaces changed this round, so both full suites ran: `apps/api` 577/578 pass (the sole failure is the already-documented pre-existing `codegen.test.ts` process-exit hang flake, stopping at the identical subtest it has in every round's log since 787, confirmed unrelated -- the new `codegen.ts` parity test itself ran and passed, both in isolation and inside this full run); `apps/web` 1111/1111 pass, no flakes. `tsc -b` (apps/web) and `npm run build` (apps/api's esbuild bundle) both clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed.

### Round 794: concurrent WhatsApp sends for one project raced the shared socket with no serialization at all

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round picked up a candidate round 744 had already identified and deliberately left open: "flagged as an open candidate for a dedicated future round, not forgotten." This is that round.

**The gap**: `WhatsAppWebManager.sendMessage` (`apps/api/src/whatsappWeb.ts`) never queued, throttled, or serialized concurrent calls for the same project -- every call went straight to `session.sock.sendMessage(...)` independently. This file's own module doc comment already discloses the real risk of the unofficial Baileys integration it wraps: "a number showing automated behavior gets flagged or temporarily blocked." A legitimate, intentionally un-suppressed workflow makes this concretely reachable: `EntityPanel.tsx`'s bulk-update "Apply to N" fires N concurrent `PATCH` requests via `Promise.allSettled`, each independently triggering `runAutomationsForRecordChange` if a matching `field_equals` rule exists.

**Why this is not deliberate**: rounds 643/644 deliberately kept automations firing normally for bulk-update (notifying real customers on a status change is the actual point of that feature, unlike CSV import's deliberate suppression of automations entirely) -- but neither round, nor any round since, ever added the missing piece: spacing the sends themselves out so "notify customers" doesn't become "blast N messages in the same instant."

**Concrete failure scenario**: a shop owner bulk-updates 50 Order rows to `status = "Shipped"`, with an enabled notify-on-status-change rule. All 50 concurrent PATCH requests independently fire the automation in well under a second, producing ~50 real outbound WhatsApp messages in a true concurrent burst on the one shared socket representing the owner's real connected number -- the exact "automated behavior" pattern this file's own comments already warn can get that number flagged or temporarily banned, a severe, business-critical outcome for an unofficial integration with no account-recovery path of its own.

**The fix**: a small per-project send queue inside `WhatsAppWebManager`, using the same Promise-chain-keyed-by-projectId idiom the class already uses for `pendingConnect`/`pendingCleanup`. Every `sendMessage()` call for a project now chains onto whatever is already queued for that project, with a fixed delay (default 1200ms, injectable via a new `sendSpacingMs` option for tests, the same way `createSocket`/`removeAuthDir` are already injectable) appended after each actual send before the next queued one goes out. Validation that never touches the socket (phone format, country-code checks) still runs immediately, unqueued -- only the real Baileys send itself (moved into a new private `performSend`, which re-reads the live session fresh since a queued call can sit behind others for a while and the connection may have dropped by the time its turn comes) is serialized. Different projects' queues stay fully independent, so one project's sends never wait behind another's.

**codegen.ts parity**: confirmed not needed -- the exported standalone app has no WhatsApp integration of any kind.

**The tests**: one new test drives three concurrent `sendMessage()` calls for the same project against a fake socket deliberately holding its own send open for a few milliseconds (unlike `createFakeSocket`'s default, which resolves instantly and could never actually observe an overlap), confirming the socket is never entered twice at once and sends land in call order. A second test confirms a slow in-flight send for one project does not block a concurrent send for a different, unrelated project.

**Verification**: both tests verified via genuine revert/restore. The serialization test fails with "3 !== 1" concurrent sends in flight when the queue chaining is reverted to always start fresh from `Promise.resolve()`; restored, it passes. The cross-project test fails (a dangling-promise test failure) when the queue is temporarily keyed by one shared key instead of per-`projectId`; restored to per-project keying, it passes. Only `apps/api` changed this round, so its own full suite ran: 579/580 pass; the sole failure is the already-documented pre-existing `codegen.test.ts` process-exit hang flake, stopping at the identical subtest it has in every round's log since 787 -- confirmed unrelated, and both new tests themselves ran and passed inside this full run. `npm run build` (esbuild bundle) clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed.
