### Round 848: a server-side arbitrary-file-write (path traversal) in the file-upload route, via an unsafe entity name -- confirmed real by reproducing the escape, then fixed

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round surfaced a genuine security vulnerability, not just a correctness bug. The survey's own candidate was the "missed sibling of an old convention sweep" pattern, explored broadly this time rather than narrowly -- it found that `apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts`'s file-upload route built its destination directory directly from `req.params.entityName`/`entity.name` with no path-containment check at all, unlike round 685's own existing defense on the READ/delete side of the same feature.

**The gap**: `createUploadMiddleware`'s own `destination` callback did `path.join(uploadsDir, req.params.id, req.params.entityName)` and immediately `mkdirSync`'d and wrote into it, with nothing checking that the result stays inside `uploadsDir`. `EntitySchema`'s own `name` field (`packages/shared/src/index.ts`) has no character-set restriction at all -- the same repeatedly-confirmed fact behind rounds 844-847's own findings. Critically, `packages/db/src/identifiers.ts`'s own `tableNameFor` -- the function that turns an entity name into a real SQL table name -- *sanitizes* an unsafe name (`replace(/[^A-Za-z0-9]/g, "_")`) rather than rejecting the build outright, so a project whose entity is literally named `"../../../tmp/evil"` still reaches `status: "built"` successfully, with that exact unsafe string preserved verbatim in `project.spec` (the sanitization only ever affects the derived SQL identifier, never the spec's own stored `entity.name`). The upload route's own `findEntity(project, req.params.entityName)` then matches that stored name exactly, and multer writes the uploaded file (up to 10 MB) wherever `path.join(uploadsDir, projectId, "../../../tmp/evil")` resolves to -- outside `uploadsDir` entirely.

**Why this is reachable, not just a theoretical string**: `encodeURIComponent` -- the exact client-side convention rounds 552 and 847 established and fixed for sending an entity name containing a `/` to the server at all -- is precisely what makes this reachable: Express decodes a `%2F` inside a single route-param segment back into a literal `/` in `req.params.entityName` before any handler runs, so a legitimately-encoded request for an entity whose name happens to contain path-traversal sequences arrives with that name intact. The round-685-era comment on this file's own `deleteUploadedFile` explicitly already documents the "entity name might not be a safe identifier" threat model for the READ/delete side (treating `entity.name` as "already-authorized" context for a *crafted file-field value*) -- but never extended the same scrutiny to entity.name's own safety as a path segment, nor to the WRITE/upload-destination side, which had no equivalent guard at all.

**Independent, empirical verification -- confirmed by actually reproducing the exploit**: wrote a test creating a project with an entity named `"../../../tmp/evil"` directly via `insertProject`/`diffAndMigrate`/`markProjectBuilt` (bypassing the AI/manual-UI paths the same way round 685's own test does), then POSTing a real file upload against it. Running this test against the *unpatched* code returned **HTTP 200** (success) -- and a real file genuinely appeared at `/tmp/evil/<uuid>.txt` on the host running this session, confirmed via a direct `ls`. This is about as concrete as "is this real" verification gets: the vulnerability was not just theoretically reachable, it was actually triggered and the escaped file was observed on disk, then immediately cleaned up (`rm -rf /tmp/evil`) before proceeding.

**The fix**: added `isPathInsideDir(candidate, dir)` (resolves both paths and checks the candidate is the dir itself or a true descendant via `path.sep`-prefixed `startsWith`) and applied it in two layers: the route's own pre-validation middleware (rejecting with a clear `400`/`UNSAFE_ENTITY_NAME` *before* multer's disk-storage middleware ever starts parsing the multipart body -- matching this exact route's own pre-existing comment stating that design goal for every other validation it already does), and, defense-in-depth, inside multer's own `destination` callback itself (in case anything ever calls `createUploadMiddleware` through a path that skips the pre-validation middleware in the future). `req.params.id` (the project id) was confirmed to need no equivalent check -- it's always a server-generated `randomUUID()`, never influenced by AI-generated or user-suppliable content the way an entity name is.

**The test**: a new `app.test.ts` test, mirroring round 685's own path-traversal test's exact structure and spirit but for the write/destination side instead of the read/delete side -- creates a project with an entity named `"../../../tmp/evil"`, confirms the upload request is rejected with `400`/`UNSAFE_ENTITY_NAME`, and confirms neither the attacker's escape target (`$TMPDIR/evil`) nor anything under the test's own sandboxed `uploadsDir` was created at all.

**Verification**: confirmed failing without the fix via the real exploit reproduction described above (not just an assertion failure -- an actual file escaping to disk), cleaned up immediately, and confirmed passing cleanly with the fix restored via a `git stash push -- apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts` / run / `git stash pop` cycle. All 12 upload-related tests in `app.test.ts` passed clean alongside the new one. `apps/api`'s own build (`esbuild src/server.ts ...`) ran clean. The full `@forge/api` suite (`npm test`) reported 598/599 passing, with the one failure being `src/codegen.test.ts` itself getting `SIGKILL`ed (confirmed via the log's own `signal: 'SIGKILL'` line) -- round 834's own previously-documented environmental memory-ceiling limitation, unrelated to this round's change (which never touches `codegen.ts`).

**Status**: shipped and pushed. `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` (the exported standalone app) has no file-upload feature at all (an established, previously-closed fact from much earlier rounds), so there is no sibling copy to port this to.

### Round 849: the same vulnerability class, found by proactively auditing round 848's own fix for missed siblings -- the delete side had an identical, unguarded path-traversal gap, and an identical stale "can never escape" comment

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey was explicitly pointed at a systematic question: round 848 fixed a path-traversal in the upload-*destination* code path (write side) -- were there other filesystem-path-building call sites using the same unrestricted `entity.name` that never got the same `isPathInsideDir` guard? The answer was yes, in the most directly analogous place possible: `deleteUploadedFile` (the per-record cleanup `deleteReplacedFileFields` triggers on a PATCH that replaces/clears a `file`-type field, or a DELETE of the record) builds `path.join(uploadsDir, projectId, entityName, filename)` and calls `rm(..., { force: true })` -- with zero containment check, even after round 848 had just added the identical check two functions away in the same file.

**Why this one is worse in one respect**: this function's own doc comment explicitly claimed the opposite -- "the project/entity directory segments come solely from this route's own already-authorized `project.id`/`entity.name`... it can never escape uploadsDir or target a different project's files" -- a claim round 848's own finding had already disproven for `entity.name` specifically, but nothing had gone back to update this comment or close the gap it was guarding against. The `filename` half of the path is also attacker-controlled: a `file`-type field's stored value is otherwise-unvalidated, client-settable JSON (confirmed directly in `packages/db`'s `repository.ts` -- `coerceValue`'s `"file"` case has no structural check at all), and only the `UPLOADED_FILENAME` regex (a bare UUID, optionally with a short extension) gates which filename segment is used -- that shape doesn't require the filename to correspond to anything this server ever actually uploaded; it's exactly the shape every legitimate upload happens to have, making this directly usable to target another project's real files by UUID.

**Independent verification before implementing**: read `deleteUploadedFile` and `deleteReplacedFileFields` directly, confirming no `isPathInsideDir` call anywhere in either. Traced both call sites (`PATCH .../entities/:entityName/:recordId` and `DELETE .../entities/:entityName/:recordId`) directly, confirming `entity` there comes from the same `findEntity`-based lookup as the upload route, so `entity.name` carries the identical "exists in the spec verbatim, no character restriction" property round 848 already established.

**The fix**: added the exact same `isPathInsideDir(target, uploadsDir)` check (the helper round 848 already added to this file) inside `deleteUploadedFile`, immediately before the `rm()` call, short-circuiting to a no-op (matching this function's own existing "best-effort, never throws" contract) rather than rejecting a request -- this function runs fire-and-forget after a response has already succeeded, so there's no request left to reject by the time it runs. Rewrote the function's own doc comment to stop claiming the now-disproven "can never escape uploadsDir" guarantee and instead describe the actual history: the prior assumption, round 848's own finding that broke it, and this round's fix.

**The test**: a new `app.test.ts` test mirroring round 685's own existing canary-file test (which defends against a crafted file-field *value* escaping) but for a traversal reached through the entity *name* instead -- creates a project with an entity named `"../../../tmp/evil"`, places a UUID-shaped canary file at that exact resolved location (standing in for "another real project's own real upload"), creates a record on that entity whose file field names that canary file, then PATCHes the field to clear it (triggering the vulnerable cleanup path) and confirms the canary survives.

**Verification, with the same empirical rigor as round 848**: running the new test against the *unpatched* code didn't just fail an assertion -- it genuinely deleted the canary file from disk, confirmed by the test's own follow-up `existsSync` check reporting `false` where `true` was expected. Restored the fix, re-ran, confirmed the canary now survives. The test's own `finally` block removes the canary directory regardless of outcome, and a direct `ls /tmp/evil` after each run confirmed no artifact was ever left behind on the host. All 13 upload-related tests in `app.test.ts` (round 685's own pre-existing path-traversal test for the crafted-value side included) passed clean alongside the two new ones from rounds 848/849. `apps/api`'s own build ran clean. The full `@forge/api` suite (`npm test`) reported 599/600 passing, the one failure being `src/codegen.test.ts`'s own already-documented `SIGKILL` environmental limitation (unrelated to this change).

**Status**: shipped and pushed. Both reachable write-path (`createUploadMiddleware`'s `destination` callback, round 848) and delete-path (`deleteUploadedFile`, round 849) filesystem-path constructions from an entity name are now guarded identically. A broader audit confirmed no other `mkdirSync`/`writeFileSync`/`rm`/`unlink` call site in `apps/api/src` builds a path from an unrestricted, spec-derived string the same way -- every other one already uses a server-generated `randomUUID()`-based segment.

### Round 850: a third instance of the same vulnerability family -- this one a READ, turning it into arbitrary-file exfiltration via WhatsApp

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. After two confirmed hits in the same root cause (rounds 848/849, both on the write/delete side), this round's survey was explicitly steered to ask whether the broader theme -- unrestricted, spec-derived strings flowing into a context that assumes they're safe -- had other untouched branches beyond filesystem writes/deletes specifically. It found one, and this instance is more severe than either of its predecessors.

**The gap**: `apps/api/src/automations.ts`'s `findTemplateFileAttachment` -- the function that lets a WhatsApp automation's message template reference a `file`-type field and have the real file attached to the outgoing message, not just its bare filename as text -- builds `path.join(uploadsDir, projectId, entity.name, storedFilename)` with no containment check, from the exact same unrestricted `entity.name` rounds 848/849 already proved exploitable. Strikingly, this function's own doc comment already says "Mirrors routes/projects.ts's own deleteUploadedFile" -- an explicit acknowledgment of the sibling relationship -- yet nobody went back to also mirror round 849's own fix to that sibling when it shipped. `storedFilename` here is even less constrained than `deleteUploadedFile`'s own version: it's just `parsed.url`'s last path segment with no `UPLOADED_FILENAME`-style shape check at all, from a `file`-type field's value that `packages/db`'s own `coerceValue` never structurally validates.

**Why this one is worse than its two siblings**: a write or delete bug corrupts or removes a file, bad enough -- but this resolved path is handed straight into `whatsappWeb.ts`'s `performSend`, which `readFile`s it and sends the raw bytes as a real WhatsApp document attachment to whatever `toNumber`/`toField` the automation rule itself names. That turns the bug into a full arbitrary-file-**read**-and-exfiltration primitive: an ordinary registered user, for their own project, can read and ship off-server the contents of any file the Node process can access -- including, in principle, this app's own multi-tenant SQLite database file, environment secrets, or another project's real uploads -- to a phone number they control. Every piece needed to trigger it (an entity name, a crafted `file`-field value, a WhatsApp automation rule) is something an ordinary project owner can set without any special privilege.

**Independent verification before implementing**: traced the full call chain directly -- `fireRule` → `findTemplateFileAttachment` → `whatsapp.sendMessage` → `performSend` → `readFile` -- confirming each step in the actual source. Confirmed `storedFilename`'s own lack of any shape validation (unlike `deleteUploadedFile`'s `UPLOADED_FILENAME` regex) by reading the function directly.

**The fix**: rather than adding a third independent copy of the containment check, extracted `isPathInsideDir` out of `routes/projects.ts` into a new shared module (`apps/api/src/uploadPaths.ts`), updated `routes/projects.ts` to import it instead of defining its own local copy, and added the same guard to `findTemplateFileAttachment` -- returning `null` (no attachment, falling back to the existing plain-text behavior) rather than throwing, matching this function's own established "silently skip past a malformed descriptor" contract for every other invalid case it already handles.

**The test**: a focused unit test (matching this function's own existing test granularity -- no server, no real WhatsApp session, no file I/O at all, since the function itself is pure path computation) confirming a traversal-named entity makes `findTemplateFileAttachment` return `null` instead of a `filePath` resolving outside `uploadsDir`.

**Verification**: confirmed failing cleanly without the fix -- the function genuinely returned `{ filePath: "/tmp/evil/abc123.pdf", ... }`, a real escaped path, as a plain string (no actual file was ever touched by this unit test, since `readFile` only happens downstream in `performSend`, which this test never calls) -- via a `git stash push -- apps/api/src/automations.ts` / run / `git stash pop` cycle, and passing with the fix restored. All 46 tests in `automations.test.ts`, all 13 upload-related tests in `app.test.ts` (confirming the `routes/projects.ts` refactor to import the shared helper broke nothing), and both attachment-related tests in `whatsappWeb.test.ts` ran clean. `apps/api`'s own build ran clean. The full `@forge/api` suite (`npm test`) reported 600/601 passing, the one failure being `src/codegen.test.ts`'s own already-documented `SIGKILL` environmental limitation.

**Status**: shipped and pushed. Three reachable call sites sharing the same root cause (write, delete, read-and-exfiltrate) are now all guarded by the same shared helper. The next round's survey is being asked to explicitly confirm this entire theme -- unrestricted spec-derived strings into a context assuming they're safe -- is now exhausted before moving to a genuinely different area.

### Round 851: the filesystem-traversal theme confirmed exhausted -- and a fresh survey immediately found a different, non-security "fix assumed a sibling was already covered" bug in the exact same file

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. As explicitly requested, this round's survey first systematically re-audited every `readFile`/`writeFile`/`mkdir`/`rm`/`unlink`/`rename`/`createReadStream`/`createWriteStream`/`stat`/`existsSync`/`appendFile`/`copyFile` call across `apps/api/src/**/*.ts`, tracing each one's path argument back to its source. Every hit either uses a server-configured path (never spec-derived) or a server-generated `randomUUID()`-based segment, or is already gated by `isPathInsideDir` (rounds 848-850). **The filesystem-traversal theme is confirmed exhausted.**

The survey then moved to a genuinely different area and found a correctness bug matching a now-familiar shape: `apps/api/src/codegen.ts`'s `handleDuplicate`/`handleBulkDuplicate` copy a `file`-type field's value verbatim into the duplicated record -- `for (const f of entity.fields) copy[f.name] = record[f.name]` -- with no special handling for `file` fields at all, unlike the live preview's own `EntityPanel.tsx`, which nulls out a file field's value on duplicate (since copying the descriptor verbatim would make the new record point at the exact same file on disk, with no "clone the file" operation to call instead) and refuses the whole operation upfront when any file field is required (since nulling it would only surface a generic required-field rejection from `createRecord` instead of a clear, actionable message).

**What makes this one notable**: `codegen.ts`'s own `requiredFileField` (computed once, already gating the Add form's own submit button) carries a doc comment that explicitly states "the live preview's own EntityPanel.tsx already guards for handleDuplicate -- this single-record Add form was the one path left unguarded." That comment is accurate about the LIVE PREVIEW (confirmed true by reading `EntityPanel.tsx` directly) but wrong about `codegen.ts` itself: `codegen.ts` is an independently-duplicated copy of the live preview's logic, not a shared implementation, so "the live preview already has this" never implies `codegen.ts`'s own copy does. A past round correctly ported the Add-form guard here while incorrectly assuming `handleDuplicate`/`handleBulkDuplicate` in this same file were already covered by virtue of the live preview having fixed its own version -- exactly the "don't trust a doc comment's claim of coverage, grep every real call site yourself" lesson this routine has already documented more than twenty times (round 671's own roadmap entry catalogs the pattern extensively), just a fresh instance of it.

**Concrete impact**: duplicating a record whose entity has a `file`-type field made the new record point at the original's own uploaded file -- and for a REQUIRED file field, silently created a record presenting as having its own signed/uploaded document it never actually received, directly circumventing the Add form's own deliberate "can't create records with a required file field in an exported app" restriction one click away via Duplicate instead.

**The fix**: mirrors `EntityPanel.tsx`'s own exact shape in both functions -- `copy[f.name] = f.type === "file" ? null : record[f.name]` for the nulling, and an upfront `if (requiredFileField) { setError(...); return; }` refusal (reusing the file's own existing `requiredFileField` variable, already in scope) before either function does anything else.

**A necessary side-effect, caught and fixed before shipping**: `requiredFileField` is a variable from the enclosing `EntityView` component's own scope -- referencing it inside `handleDuplicate`/`handleBulkDuplicate` is fine in the REAL generated code (ordinary closure), but four existing `codegen.test.ts` tests extract these two functions' source via regex and execute them standalone via `new Function(...)` with an explicit, named parameter list that never included `requiredFileField`. Running those tests unmodified against the new code would throw `ReferenceError: requiredFileField is not defined` the moment either function's body referenced it. Updated all four call sites to add `requiredFileField` as a new parameter (passing `undefined`, since none of those tests' own fixture entities have a file field, preserving their existing behavior exactly) -- confirmed all four still pass.

**The test**: two new `codegen.test.ts` tests, using the same regex-extraction-and-execute technique as the file's existing `handleDuplicate`/`handleBulkDuplicate` tests -- one confirming a file field's value comes back `null` on the copy (for both the single and bulk paths), one confirming `createRecord` is never called at all when the entity has a required file field (again both paths), with the single-record case also confirming the surfaced error names the blocking field.

**Verification**: confirmed failing cleanly without the fix -- the file-nulling test showed the original's own full JSON descriptor passed through unchanged where `null` was expected, and the required-field test showed `createRecord` genuinely getting called where it should have been refused -- via a `git stash push -- apps/api/src/codegen.ts` / run / `git stash pop` cycle, and passing with the fix restored. All 8 Duplicate-related tests (the 2 new ones, the 4 updated-parameter ones, and 2 more pre-existing ones) passed clean, plus the esbuild syntax-validity check (no backtick-escaping mistake this time). `node --check` on `codegen.ts` and `apps/web`'s `tsc -b` (untouched this round, run as a sanity check) both came back clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed, `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` only -- `apps/web/src/EntityPanel.tsx` already had this fix, which is precisely what this round ported from.

### Round 852: the Duplicate fix's own "live preview already has this" lesson repeats one level down -- round 798's CREATE-only required-file-field guard never covered editing an existing record

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. With the filesystem-traversal theme confirmed exhausted (round 851) and the file-type-field-aware-logic cross-check (`FieldInput`/`Cell`/CSV export/`matchesSearch`/`buildImportRecords`/`bulkEditableFields`, plus now `handleDuplicate`/`handleBulkDuplicate`) also confirmed fully mirrored across every site this round's survey could find, the survey turned to re-examining round 798's own fix itself rather than its siblings -- and found the fix's own reasoning had a gap it never noticed.

**The gap**: round 798 added a CREATE-only guard (`editingId == null && requiredFileField`) to `codegen.ts`'s exported `EntityView`, reasoning that "an existing record that already has a file ... keeps form[f.name] non-empty, so editing its OTHER fields is still possible." That's true only for a record created *after* the field became required. `packages/db/src/migrate.ts`'s own comment already states the relevant fact plainly: "NOT NULL deliberately omitted: SQLite can't retroactively satisfy it against a table's existing rows ... The column is added nullable; required-ness is still enforced by the API for every write going forward." Flipping a field's `required` flag via refine never backfills existing rows -- a record that predates the refine keeps whatever it had before, which can be `null`. `startEdit`'s own seeding (`next[f.name] = record[f.name] ?? (f.type === "boolean" ? false : "")`) turns that stored `null` into `form[f.name] = ""` the moment such a record is opened for editing. The exported app's own `FieldInput` file-type branch renders only a static `<a>`/`<span>` display plus a disclaimer paragraph -- confirmed via direct read, there is no `onChange` anywhere in that branch, so `form[f.name]` can never become non-empty here no matter what the user does. The generic, unconditional `missingField` check (`entity.fields.find((f) => f.required && (form[f.name] === "" || form[f.name] == null))`) then fires on every single submit attempt -- permanently blocking a save of that record, even one that only changes a completely unrelated field, behind a message ("is a required field") that reads like a fixable omission rather than the dead end round 798 itself already named and solved for the CREATE path alone.

**Why this is the same lesson as round 851's `handleDuplicate`, one level down**: round 798's own fix assumed its own reasoning ("an existing record already has a file") covered the EDIT path without separately checking whether that assumption actually holds for every record an EDIT could reach -- the same "proximity/doc-comment claims coverage" fallacy this routine has now caught repeatedly (round 850's `findTemplateFileAttachment`, round 851's `handleDuplicate`/`handleBulkDuplicate`), just surfacing here as an unstated premise in the original fix's own prose rather than a comment pointing elsewhere.

**The fix**: replaced the CREATE-only check with a new derived value, `recordHasNoRequiredFile`, keyed on the *current form value* rather than `editingId` -- `requiredFileField && (form[requiredFileField.name] === "" || form[requiredFileField.name] == null)` -- so a record that genuinely does have a file keeps editing its other fields unaffected, exactly as round 798's own original reasoning intended for that case. This value now gates all three places round 798's fix touched: `handleSubmit`'s early check (with a ternary message distinguishing "can't be created" from "has no file for its required ... field, and files can't be added in an exported app"), the explanatory `<p role="alert">` banner above the form, and the disabled Save/Add button.

**Confirmed not a behavioral regression**: disabling Save for an entire broken record (not just blocking that one field) was deliberately considered and rejected as a concern -- the generic `missingField` check already unconditionally blocked any save on that record before this fix too; the fix only makes the reason visible and consistent with the CREATE path's own established UX (explanatory banner plus disabled button) rather than changing what was or wasn't actually possible.

**The test**: a new `codegen.test.ts` test mirroring round 798's own existing CREATE-path test's structure exactly -- builds an "Applicant" entity with a required `file` field ("Resume"), mocks a GET returning one existing record whose `resume` value is `null` (simulating a record that predates the field becoming required), clicks the real generated `<button onClick={() => startEdit(r)}>Edit</button>` to enter edit mode, confirms the Save button is disabled and the specific "has no file for its required" message is already visible without needing to attempt a submit first, then changes the unrelated "name" field and submits anyway -- confirming no PATCH ever fires and the surfaced error is the EDIT-specific wording, not the CREATE-only or generic one.

**Verification**: confirmed failing cleanly without the fix -- via a `git stash push -- apps/api/src/codegen.ts` / run / `git stash pop` cycle (leaving the test file in place) -- Save was enabled and the record saved successfully with the "no file" state intact, none of the new guard text present. Passing with the fix restored. Re-ran the full required-file-field/Duplicate test set together (10 tests: round 798's CREATE test, all 8 Duplicate-related tests from round 851, and this round's new EDIT test) -- all passed clean, confirming no interaction regression across the three rounds that have now touched this same `requiredFileField` area. The esbuild syntax-validity check and `node --check` on both `codegen.ts` and `codegen.test.ts` all came back clean. `apps/web`'s own `tsc -b` (untouched this round, run as a sanity check) also came back clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed, `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` only -- the live preview's own `apps/web/src/EntityPanel.tsx` has no equivalent restriction to begin with (it supports real file uploads directly, so a required file field is never permanently unsatisfiable there), so there is no sibling to check this against.

### Round 853: a refine that drops an entity never purged that entity's own localStorage preferences -- the same "missed sibling" shape as rounds 390-401, one level down from whole-project deletion

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. With both the filesystem-traversal theme (848-850) and the file-type-field-aware-logic cross-check (798/851/852) confirmed exhausted, this round's survey looked for a different recurring shape -- a fix applied at one lifecycle granularity (the whole project) never generalized to a narrower one (a single entity within a surviving project) -- and found exactly that in `App.tsx`'s own `handleBuildComplete`.

**The gap**: `handleBuildComplete`'s own comment already explicitly reasons about one consequence of a refine dropping an entity (an instruction like "remove deals tracking, focus on invoices" -- see `routes/projects.ts`'s own comment on `/refine`): the stale `activeEntity` tab going blank, which it fixes by falling back to the first remaining entity. But it does nothing about that dropped entity's own per-entity-keyed localStorage preferences. Across `columnWidths.ts`, `columnOrder.ts`, `columnVisibility.ts`, `fieldFiltersPreference.ts`, `groupByPreference.ts` (plus its paired field-type store), `collapsedBoardColumnsPreference.ts`, `collapsedGroupsPreference.ts`, `sortKeysPreference.ts`, `viewModePreference.ts`, and `entityRecentSearches.ts`, every one exports a `purge...ForProject(projectId)` used only by `projectPreferenceCleanup.ts` on actual project deletion -- confirmed by grepping every `purge*ForProject` name and every `purgeProjectPreferences` call site in `App.tsx`/`EntityPanel.tsx` directly, finding no narrower, per-entity call path anywhere.

**Why this is reachable, not theoretical**: refine is the app's flagship, everyday feature, and before a refine drops an entity, a real user interacting with it in `EntityPanel.tsx` normally populates several of these stores -- dragging/resizing/hiding columns, setting filters, grouping, sorting, picking Board/Calendar view, collapsing groups -- this app's main per-entity customization surface, not an edge case. The entries then sit in localStorage forever, exactly the "a missed store leaks without bound" shape rounds 390/392/399/401 already fixed at whole-project granularity, just one level down. Worse than a pure leak: several of these stores (`columnOrder`/`columnWidths`/hidden fields/`entityRecentSearches`) have no type-check at all, so if a later refine reintroduces an entity with the exact same name but a different field shape, the stale preference silently reapplies to the new, unrelated entity.

**The fix**: added a `purge...ForEntity(projectId, entityName)` to each of the eight files that lacked one (`columnWidths.ts`'s own `clearColumnWidths` and `entityRecentSearches.ts`'s own `clearEntityRecentSearches` already existed, originally for an unrelated "reset to default" UI action, and are reused as-is), using exact-key deletion for the two-segment-keyed stores and `${projectId}:${entityName}:`-prefix deletion for the two three-segment-keyed stores (`collapsedBoardColumnsPreference.ts`/`collapsedGroupsPreference.ts`, whose key also carries a board/group field name). A new `entityPreferenceCleanup.ts` mirrors `projectPreferenceCleanup.ts`'s own shape and doc-comment style, exporting a single `purgeEntityPreferences(projectId, entityName)` that calls all ten. `handleBuildComplete` now captures the pre-refine entity list (via the `project` state variable, read before `setProject` overwrites it) right alongside its own existing `activeEntity` fix, diffs it against the newly-built spec, and calls `purgeEntityPreferences` for every entity present before but absent after.

**A necessary side-effect, caught during verification**: two pre-existing `App.test.ts` tests extract `handleBuildComplete`'s real source via regex and execute it standalone via `new Function(...)` with an explicit, named parameter list -- the exact `new Function` extraction-test fragility round 851 already hit in `codegen.test.ts`. Referencing the new `project` free variable inside the real function broke both with `ReferenceError: project is not defined` the moment either ran. Fixed by adding `project` and `purgeEntityPreferences` as new parameters (passing `null`/a no-op stub, since neither existing test's own focus is this round's new behavior) to both call sites -- confirmed both still pass, preserving their original assertions unchanged.

**The tests**: a new `entityPreferenceCleanup.test.ts`, mirroring `projectPreferenceCleanup.test.ts`'s own exact shape and rigor -- seeds every store for the entity being dropped, a SIBLING entity in the SAME project (must survive, since only one entity was dropped), and the SAME entity name in an UNRELATED project (must also survive) -- using the real public read functions every other part of the app uses, not a mock of each store. A new `App.test.ts` test confirms `handleBuildComplete` itself calls `purgeEntityPreferences` once per actually-dropped entity, with the built project's own id, and never for an entity that survived the refine.

**Verification**: confirmed both new tests fail cleanly without the fix -- `entityPreferenceCleanup.test.ts` with a `Cannot find module` error (the whole new module stashed away) and the `App.test.ts` purge-wiring test with an empty call list where two purge calls were expected -- via `git stash push -u` cycles (the new untracked `entityPreferenceCleanup.ts` included via `-u`, the test files left in place), and passing with the fix restored. The full `apps/web` suite (`npm test`, 1143 tests) reported 1142 passing, the one failure being an i18n translation gap (round 854, below) confirmed independently pre-existing and unrelated via the same stash-cycle technique. `apps/web`'s own `tsc -b` ran clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed, `apps/web` only -- `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` (the exported standalone app) has no localStorage-based per-entity preference system of its own to begin with (an already-established fact from earlier rounds' localStorage-staleness series), so there is no sibling to port this to. One related, lower-severity leak was noted but deliberately left out of scope: `entityTabOrder.ts` is keyed by `projectId` alone (a list of entity names, not `${projectId}:${entityName}`), and a dropped entity's name lingers in that list -- but `applyColumnOrder`'s own self-healing (any name not matching a current field/entity is simply ignored, with real entities appended in their own natural order) means this is a pure, harmless storage leak with none of this round's "silently reapplies to the wrong new entity" risk, unlike the other nine. Left as a candidate for a future round if the localStorage-staleness series is revisited.

### Round 855: `coerceValue`'s own default branch (text/longtext/file) had no rejection path at all, unlike every sibling case in the same function -- the exact same gap round 546 already fixed one case above, just never reached this one

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. With rounds 853/854 closing out the localStorage-preference-cleanup series, this round's survey went back to a different recurring shape: a fix already applied to several sibling branches within one function, but not to every branch that needed it. It found exactly that inside `packages/db/src/repository.ts`'s own `coerceValue` -- the single choke point every record write in this app funnels through (`insertRecord`/`updateRecord`, called directly with `req.body` by `routes/projects.ts` with no schema validation above them).

**The gap**: `coerceValue`'s `switch (field.type)` has an explicit, commented rejection path for every type with its own `case` -- `number`/`relation` rejects an array or a non-finite number, `boolean` rejects anything outside the exact true/false allowlist (round 546's own fix), `enum` rejects a value outside `enumValues`, `date` rejects a malformed date string. The `default` branch -- every field type with no explicit `case`, meaning `text`, `longtext`, and `file` -- had none of this: `return String(raw);` with no type check at all. `String({ foo: "bar" })` is the literal string `"[object Object]"`; `String([1, 2, 3])` is `"1,2,3"`. Both "succeed" silently, writing garbage to the field with the request still reporting 200/201.

**Why this is reachable, not theoretical**: `apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts` passes `req.body` straight into `insertRecord` (line 1935) and `updateRecord` (line 2767) with no per-field-shape Zod schema above `coerceValue` -- confirmed by reading both call sites directly. A direct API call (a script, a third-party integration against this app's own documented REST API, or a future client bug that accidentally sends a parsed object instead of a string) hitting a text/longtext/file field with an object or array value gets it silently corrupted instead of a clear 400. Verified independently by calling `insertRecord` directly against a real in-memory database with `{ notes: { foo: "bar" } }` and `{ notes: [1, 2, 3] }` -- both wrote the stringified garbage with no error, before the fix.

**Why a legitimate `file` field value is never at risk from the fix**: a `file`-type field's real value is always a plain JSON-stringified string by the time it reaches `coerceValue` -- the upload route's own doc comment states this explicitly ("the caller then PATCHes/POSTs that descriptor, JSON-stringified, as the field's own value, exactly like every other record write"), and every real upload test in `app.test.ts` was confirmed (via grep) to already send `JSON.stringify(file)`, never the raw descriptor object.

**The fix**: added a `typeof raw !== "string" && typeof raw !== "number" && typeof raw !== "boolean"` check to the default branch, throwing the same `ValidationError` every sibling case already uses -- allowing a number or boolean literal through unchanged (matching `enum`'s/`date`'s own existing laxness, which already call `String(raw)` without a `typeof` gate), rejecting only an object or array.

**The test**: a new `repository.test.ts` test mirroring round 546's own boolean-rejection test exactly -- confirms `insertRecord` throws `ValidationError` for a `text` field given `{ foo: "bar" }`, `[1, 2, 3]`, `[]`, or `{}`.

**Verification**: confirmed failing cleanly without the fix -- `insertRecord` genuinely wrote `"[object Object]"` to the field with no error thrown -- via a `git stash push -- packages/db/src/repository.ts` / run / `git stash pop` cycle, and passing with the fix restored. The full `@forge/db` suite (218 tests) ran clean. `apps/api`'s own full `app.test.ts` (236 tests, not the SIGKILL-prone `codegen.test.ts`) ran clean, confirming every real upload-flow test's existing `JSON.stringify(file)` convention is genuinely unaffected. `apps/api`'s own build ran clean.

**Also ported to `apps/api/src/codegen.ts`**: the exported standalone app has its own independently-duplicated copy of this exact function (`coerce`, confirmed via direct read to have the identical shape -- number/relation/boolean/enum/date each with their own guard, then an unguarded `return String(value);` fallthrough), reached the same way (`req.body?.[f.name]` flowing straight into `coerce` with nothing else validating it first, confirmed at both its create and update call sites). Added the identical `typeof` guard. A new `codegen.test.ts` test, following this file's own established "spawn a real generated `server.js`, POST/PATCH against it over real HTTP" standard for testing this exact function (matching round 546's own sibling boolean test for `coerce`), confirmed failing without the fix (a real spawned server returned 201 for an object-valued text field) and passing with it restored. All 6 of this file's own "generated server.js rejects..." tests ran together clean, plus the esbuild syntax-validity check and `node --check` on both files.

**Status**: shipped and pushed, both `packages/db/src/repository.ts` (the live app) and `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` (the exported app) -- the one function in each with this exact shape, now at full parity with every sibling branch.

### Round 856: `FieldSchema` never validated that a field `name` is a safe SQL identifier -- only two specific reserved words were ever rejected, unlike an entity name's own general sanitization

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey was explicitly asked to find a genuinely new angle after several rounds mining very similar veins (file-field handling, path safety, `coerceValue` siblings). It found one by re-examining `packages/shared/src/index.ts`'s own `FieldSchema` against `packages/db/src/identifiers.ts`'s `assertSafeIdentifier` -- the same "every sibling already has this guard, one branch doesn't" shape, just at the schema-validation layer this time instead of inside a single function's switch statement.

**The gap**: every field name reaching `fieldColumns()` (`repository.ts:155`) or the column loop in `migrate.ts` (four call sites) is passed straight into `assertSafeIdentifier(field.name, "column")`, which throws a raw `Error` unless the name matches `^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]*$` exactly. An entity name gets the same assert, but `tableNameFor` always sanitizes it first (replacing every non-ASCII-alphanumeric character with `_`) -- so an entity name, however exotic, never actually throws there. A field name gets no such preprocessing anywhere: it reaches the assert completely raw. `FieldSchema` itself only rejected the two literal reserved words `id`/`createdAt` (`RESERVED_FIELD_NAMES`) -- it had no general check that `name` is shaped like a safe identifier at all.

**Why this is reachable, not theoretical, and already half-acknowledged in the codebase**: the only thing stopping an unsafe field name from reaching this crash point was a soft prompt instruction to the LLM ("Every entity/field name MUST stay a plain ASCII identifier" -- `packages/spec-engine/src/anthropic.ts`/`debug.ts`), never enforced server-side; `AnthropicSpecProvider.generate()`/`requestSpecFix()` both validate the model's JSON with nothing but `ProductSpecSchema.safeParse`. Even more tellingly, `routes/projects.ts`'s own `deriveFieldName` (the manual "add field" UI path) has a comment explicitly documenting this exact gap, found and closed for that ONE call path at round 549: "passes FieldSchema (no identifier-shape guard) but throws a raw 'Unsafe column identifier' error from assertSafeIdentifier the moment the project is actually built." Round 549 fixed the symptom for the manual UI (by having `deriveFieldName` always produce a safe camelCase name derived from the label) but never closed the actual gap at the schema itself -- so the AI provider's raw JSON output, which never goes through `deriveFieldName` at all, remained exposed the entire time. This is precisely the documented design principle `RESERVED_FIELD_NAMES`'s own comment states ("better a spec falls back to the heuristic provider than reach either database layer with an unreconcilable name"), just never generalized from two specific names to the actual underlying hazard its own reasoning describes.

**The fix**: added a `FieldSchema` refine requiring `name` to match `/^[A-Za-z][A-Za-z0-9_]*$/` -- the identical `SAFE_FIELD_NAME` regex duplicated locally (matching this file's own established convention for `findSanitizedIdentifierCollisions`, since `@forge/shared` can't depend on `@forge/db`) -- with a message pointing the user at `label` for a human-facing display name instead.

**A necessary test-fixture fix, caught during verification**: `apps/api/src/pipeline.test.ts`'s own `brokenSpec` deliberately uses an unsafe field name (`"name; DROP TABLE x;--"`) to force a real `diffAndMigrate` failure, for its three Debug-Agent-recovery tests. `insertProject` always round-trips its argument through `getProject`, which calls `ProductSpecSchema.parse` -- so storing `brokenSpec` directly now throws immediately, before the test even reaches `runBuildPipeline`. Traced `runBuildPipeline`'s own signature to confirm `previousSpec` comes from `options.previousSpec` (never from the stored `project.spec`) and that `nextSpec` is handed straight to `diffAndMigrate` with no re-validation against the schema -- meaning the stored project spec and the "spec about to be built" are two genuinely independent values in this test. Fixed by storing the already-safe `fixedSpec` instead, while still passing `brokenSpec` as `nextSpec` -- preserving every one of the three tests' original intent (the real migration failure still happens, Debug Agent still has to recover from it) with no change to any assertion.

**The tests**: two new `index.test.ts` tests mirroring the existing `RESERVED_FIELD_NAMES` test cluster's own exact style -- one confirming rejection for a space, a hyphen, a leading digit, and a Hebrew name; one confirming acceptance for every shape a real field name already uses (leading letter, digits, underscores).

**Verification**: confirmed failing cleanly without the fix -- `FieldSchema.safeParse({ name: "due date", ... })` genuinely succeeded where rejection was expected -- via a `git stash push -- packages/shared/src/index.ts` / run / `git stash pop` cycle, and passing with the fix restored. Full `@forge/shared` (18 tests), `@forge/db` (218 tests), and `@forge/spec-engine` (163 tests, confirming every deterministic heuristic/template generator already produces safe field names) suites all ran clean. `apps/api`'s full suite (444 tests, every file except the SIGKILL-prone `codegen.test.ts`) ran clean, including all 31 of `pipeline.test.ts`'s own tests after the fixture fix. `apps/web`'s full suite ran clean except `BuildProgress.test.ts`'s own already-documented recurring flake (confirmed unrelated by re-running that file alone: 34/34 passing). `apps/api`'s build and `apps/web`'s `tsc -b` both ran clean. A broad repo-wide grep for any other test fixture using a space-containing, non-ASCII, or special-character field name (as opposed to entity name, which is deliberately exempt) turned up only the two already-handled cases (`migrate.test.ts`'s own direct, schema-bypassing call to `generateCreateTableStatements`, confirmed unaffected since it never touches `FieldSchema`, and `pipeline.test.ts`, fixed above).

**Status**: shipped and pushed, `packages/shared/src/index.ts` only -- the one point every spec (heuristic, AI provider, its own repair path, and the manual UI, which already produced a compliant name on its own) is validated.

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey was explicitly asked to find a genuinely new angle after several rounds mining very similar veins. It found one in `apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts`'s own rate-limiter wiring: `/auth/signup`, `/auth/login`, and `/auth/forgot-password` each have their own `createRateLimiter` instance (IP-keyed for the first two, email-keyed for the third), with a shared comment block explaining exactly why each one is needed. `/auth/login/verify-code` -- registered a few lines below `/auth/login`, and the one route that actually completes the email-code login flow `/auth/login` starts -- had none, with no comment anywhere explaining why it was left out (unlike `/auth/reset-password`, whose own lack of a limiter IS explicitly documented and justified elsewhere in this codebase).

**Why this needed care, not just a reflexive copy-paste of the pattern**: the obvious first read -- "an unguarded code-verification endpoint, brute-forceable" -- turned out to be the WRONG framing on closer inspection. `MAX_LOGIN_CODE_ATTEMPTS` (a constant already set to 5) already caps wrong guesses against one specific `loginCodeId` row permanently, independent of request rate or time window: the row is deleted after the 5th wrong guess, full stop. A sliding-window rate limiter keyed the same way (`loginCodeId`) would be pure redundancy with a cap that's already strictly tighter. The actual, still-real gap this round confirmed by reading `generateLoginCode`/`hashLoginCode`'s own comments directly is different: this is the cheapest unauthenticated POST endpoint in the entire API to call repeatedly (`sha256` + `timingSafeEqual`, deliberately not scrypt, per this file's own comment explaining why a fast hash is fine here specifically because the attempt cap is the real defense) -- so unlike the guessing risk, the plain **request-volume** risk (flooding this route with garbage `loginCodeId` values, each costing a real DB lookup) was never actually addressed by anything, the same volumetric concern every sibling route in this exact file already has a limiter for.

**The fix**: added `verifyLoginCodeRateLimiter`, mirroring `loginRateLimiter`'s own exact shape (IP-keyed, same window/max) -- matching signup/login's own stated rationale ("one machine iterating quickly is the realistic attack shape") rather than forgot-password's email-keying (there's no single "victim inbox" analog here to protect). Extended the shared comment block above all four limiters to explain the distinction between this fix (a request-volume throttle) and the pre-existing, independent, permanent per-row attempt cap (a guessing defense) -- so a future reader doesn't mistake one for doing the other's job.

**The test**: a new `app.test.ts` test mirroring the existing `/auth/login`/`/auth/forgot-password` rate-limit tests' own exact style -- signs up, logs in to mint a real `loginCodeId`, fires 30 wrong-code requests against it (confirming none of them are `429` yet -- the exact response code for each one doesn't matter, since the row's own 5-attempt cap means some land as `INVALID_LOGIN_CODE` and some as `LOGIN_CODE_EXPIRED` once it's deleted, which is irrelevant to what this test is actually checking), then confirms the 31st is rejected with `429`/`RATE_LIMITED`.

**Verification**: confirmed failing cleanly without the fix -- the 31st request returned `401`, not `429` -- via a `git stash push -- apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts` / run / `git stash pop` cycle, and passing with the fix restored. Ran the full auth-related test cluster (19 tests, explicitly including the existing "locks it out after too many wrong attempts" test, confirming the two independent defenses -- the new volumetric limiter and the pre-existing per-row attempt cap -- don't interfere with each other) and the full `app.test.ts` suite (237 tests) both clean. `apps/api`'s build ran clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed, `apps/api/src/routes/auth.ts` only -- `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` (the exported standalone app) has no auth system of its own at all (confirmed via grep), so there is no sibling to port this to.

### Round 858: `routes/projects.ts`'s real, metered AI-generation routes had no rate limiter at all -- a gap round 807 already found and documented, but never actually fixed in code

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey found a gap in the same general family as round 857 (unauthenticated-vs-authenticated rate limiting), but in a different file and for a genuinely different reason: cost control and cross-user denial-of-service, not credential-guessing or email-bombing. `routes/auth.ts` now has a limiter on every one of its unauthenticated routes (rounds 847-857). `routes/projects.ts` -- which spends real, metered Anthropic API cost on `/ideas/enhance`, `POST /projects`, `.../answers`, and `.../refine` every single call whenever `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is configured (which it is for this app's real deployment; only an unconfigured deployment falls back to the free heuristic provider) -- had none at all.

**Not a newly-discovered gap -- a previously-documented one that was never actually closed**: round 807's own fix to `docs/security.md` explicitly states, in its own verification notes, "confirmed the inverse -- `routes/projects.ts`/`app.ts` never import `createRateLimiter` at all, so `POST /api/projects`/`.../refine` genuinely remain unprotected" -- but that round's own scope was docs-only (correcting what the security doc claimed, not fixing the underlying code), and no round since (verified via `git log` and a fresh grep against the current tree) ever came back to close the code gap itself.

**Why this matters, precisely**: every route in this file already sits behind `requireAuth`, so this isn't an anonymous-abuse gap -- but an authenticated account looping any of these calls has nothing to stop it. `activePipelines` (the only existing guard near these routes) is a `Set<projectId>` that exists purely to block two overlapping requests on the SAME project from racing each other (lost-update protection); it does nothing to stop one account calling `/ideas/enhance` or creating/refining many projects in a tight sequential loop. Impact is twofold: unbounded real-dollar cost to whoever holds the deployment's API key, and a genuine denial-of-service for every OTHER user, since Anthropic's own account-level rate limits are shared across the whole deployment -- one abusive account burning through them makes every other user's `/build`/`/refine` start failing too.

**The fix**: one shared `createRateLimiter` instance (reusing the exact helper already proven out in `routes/auth.ts`), applied to `/ideas/enhance`, `POST /projects`, `.../answers`, and `.../refine` -- deliberately ONE limiter across all four rather than one per route, since they're really a single budget ("how many real AI-generation calls can this account trigger"), not four independent concerns; a caller alternating between routes to dodge a per-route cap is still correctly caught by the shared counter. Keyed by user id (not IP, unlike `routes/auth.ts`'s signup/login limiters), since every caller here is already authenticated and a shared IP (an office, a NAT) must never collaterally throttle an unrelated account.

**Deliberately excludes `/build`**: traced its own handler directly rather than accepting the survey's first-pass claim that it also "calls through to generateSpec" -- `/build` actually reuses the spec `POST /projects`/`.../answers` already generated (`nextSpec: project.spec`), and only ever makes its own extra AI call on the rare Debug Agent repair path (`streamPipeline`'s own single-shot `requestSpecFix`, triggered only by a genuine migration failure, confirmed by re-reading `pipeline.ts` directly: no retry loop, at most one repair attempt per build). Counting an ordinary build -- zero extra AI cost in the common case -- against the same budget as an actual spec generation would eat into a legitimate user's allowance for no real cost reason.

**The test**: a new `app.test.ts` test confirming the shared-budget design specifically, not just "a limiter exists" -- calls `/ideas/enhance` 30 times for one account (none rate-limited), then calls the 31st request against a DIFFERENT route (`POST /projects`) and confirms THAT one is rejected with `429`/`RATE_LIMITED` (proving the counter is genuinely shared across routes, not per-route), then confirms a completely different account gets its own fresh allowance immediately after.

**Verification**: confirmed failing cleanly without the fix -- the 31st cross-route call returned `201`, not `429` -- via a `git stash push -- apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts` / run / `git stash pop` cycle, and passing with the fix restored. The full `app.test.ts` suite (238 tests) ran clean. `apps/api`'s build ran clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed, `apps/api/src/routes/projects.ts` only -- `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` (the exported standalone app) has no AI-generation feature of its own at all (confirmed via grep), so there is no sibling to port this to.

### Round 859: the automation webhook action's own SSRF guard was defeated in one hop by an ordinary HTTP redirect -- the single most common real-world SSRF bypass technique

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey re-examined `automations.ts`'s own `isAllowedWebhookUrl` -- one of the most heavily-hardened functions in this codebase, incrementally tightened across multiple prior rounds to cover IPv4/IPv6 private ranges, IPv4-mapped/NAT64-encoded literals, and the real CIDR shape of `fc00::/7`/`fe80::/10` rather than their single literal hex group -- and found that every bit of that investment is defeated in one hop by a technique none of it ever touches.

**The gap**: `fireWebhookAction` calls `isAllowedWebhookUrl(rule.webhookUrl)` exactly once, before ever calling `fetch`. The `fetch` call itself passed no `redirect` option, so Node's own `fetch` (undici) used its default of `"follow"` -- silently following up to 20 redirects, re-requesting whatever `Location` header a 3xx response names, with zero re-validation against `isAllowedWebhookUrl` on the final destination. `rule.webhookUrl` is entirely user-supplied (any project collaborator can type one in, per this file's own comment); an attacker only needs to control or compromise any ordinary PUBLIC HTTP(S) endpoint -- trivially passing the hostname check, since it's a normal public hostname -- then respond to the webhook's POST with a redirect to the cloud instance-metadata address (`169.254.169.254`, explicitly named in this file's own comment as "the single most common real-world SSRF target") or any other address `isAllowedWebhookUrl` would otherwise block.

**Why this is worse than the gap the code already discloses**: `isAllowedWebhookUrl`'s own comment already states this is "not full SSRF-proofing (no DNS-rebinding protection...)" -- an honest, deliberate limitation, since DNS rebinding requires winning a timing race against DNS TTL/caching, genuinely hard to defend against with a plain `fetch` call. An HTTP redirect needs none of that: it's synchronous, deterministic, requires no race condition and no DNS control at all -- strictly easier to pull off than the already-disclosed gap, and a well-known, textbook SSRF bypass technique, not a novel or sophisticated one.

**The fix**: added `redirect: "manual"` to the one `fetch` call. Verified empirically (a real local HTTP server returning a genuine 302) that with this option, Node's `fetch` returns the raw 3xx response instead of following it -- `status`/`ok` reflect the redirect response itself, not an opaque browser-only type that only applies to no-cors cross-origin requests -- so the function's own pre-existing `res.ok ? "sent" : "failed"` check already treats an unfollowed redirect exactly like any other non-2xx failure, with no further code change needed. Updated `isAllowedWebhookUrl`'s own comment, which previously named "no redirect-following check on the response" as a known limitation -- no longer true after this fix.

**The tests**: two new `automations.test.ts` tests -- one asserting the real call site's fetch options include `redirect: "manual"` (the actual regression-sensitive assertion, mirroring this file's own existing "mock `globalThis.fetch`, inspect the call" convention), one confirming a mocked 3xx response is correctly recorded as a failed automation run, not success (documenting the already-correct downstream handling, which the first test's fix makes actually apply to a real redirect rather than one undici silently absorbed).

**Verification**: confirmed failing cleanly without the fix -- the fetch call's own `init.redirect` was `undefined`, not `"manual"` -- via a `git stash push -- apps/api/src/automations.ts` / run / `git stash pop` cycle, and passing with the fix restored. The full `automations.test.ts` (48 tests), `app.test.ts`, and `pipeline.test.ts` suites (317 tests total) ran clean. `apps/api`'s build ran clean. A repo-wide grep confirmed this is the ONLY server-side `fetch` call in `apps/api/src` targeting a user-supplied URL -- no other sibling call site exists needing the same fix.

**Status**: shipped and pushed, `apps/api/src/automations.ts` only -- `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` (the exported standalone app) has no automations/webhook feature of its own at all (confirmed via grep), so there is no sibling to port this to.

### Round 860: a required relation field whose target entity never existed got no FK and no diagnostic for a brand-new column/table -- the exact candidate round 415 tried and reverted, this time with the distinguishing mechanism that revert explicitly asked for

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey proposed re-implementing a ProductSpecSchema-level hard rejection of any spec with an unresolvable `relationTo` -- **exactly the candidate round 415 already tried, found broke a deliberate, long-standing feature, and explicitly reverted**, with its own closing note stating in plain terms: "must not be re-attempted without a way to distinguish an intentional 'entity may not exist yet' placeholder... from a genuine AI-generated mismatch." Independent verification confirmed this is indeed a re-proposal, not a new finding -- but also surfaced that round 415's own revert note left the door open for exactly this topic if a genuine distinguishing mechanism were ever found, and reading the actual code turned one up.

**What round 415 found and reverted**: `domainEntities.ts`'s own built-in library deliberately keeps a relation field's `relationTo` naming an entity that may not be included in a given generated spec (`Order.courierId -> "Courier"`), with its own comment explaining why `null` is a legitimate, honest value for "not assigned yet" -- forcing the reference or blocking the build would be worse. A hard schema-level reject can't structurally distinguish that deliberate placeholder from a genuine typo or a refine that renamed/removed the real target entity; both look identical (a `relationTo` string with no matching entity name), so round 415's fix broke 10 heuristic-provider tests and was reverted in full.

**The distinguishing signal this round found**: read every single `relationTo` declaration in `domainEntities.ts` directly (not just the one example round 415's own note cited) -- all five are `required: false`, confirming the deliberate-placeholder pattern this file uses is *always* optional, for exactly the reason its own comment states (a required field with an invalid reference has no honest value to hold; an optional one can legitimately stay empty). A REQUIRED relation field whose target doesn't exist at all has no such legitimate interpretation anywhere in this codebase's own established conventions -- it's a genuine gap, not a feature, every time.

**The fix, deliberately NOT round 415's approach**: rather than a schema-level hard rejection (which broke the deliberate pattern precisely because it can't see `required`), this adds a non-blocking hazard note -- the existing `describeMigrationHazards` mechanism, already surfaced in the Architect's build/refine warning message and the checkpoint-restore route -- scoped to `required: true` relation fields only. Since the domain library's own placeholder pattern is always optional, this new diagnostic can never fire for it; the build/refine/restore flow never fails, nothing round 415 found is at risk of breaking again, yet the genuinely dangerous case (a required field permanently unsatisfiable, previously invisible) is now surfaced. Extended `generateCreateTableStatements`'s/the new-column ALTER branch's own silent `fk = ""` fallback with a new shared helper, wired into all three places a brand-new relation column/table can appear: the very first build (`previousSpec` undefined -- the single most common case, every `/build` call), a brand-new entity added by a refine, and a brand-new field added to an already-existing entity by a refine. Reworded the existing `relation_missing_fk` message (previously "reusing a column," not true for this new case) to stay accurate for both root causes, and added a `relationToNeverExisted` flag on `MigrationChange` to distinguish them going forward.

**Confirmed via direct code read, not accepted on the subagent's claim**: traced `generateCreateTableStatements` (silently drops the REFERENCES clause), both the brand-new-table and new-column branches in `diffAndMigrate` (neither runs any per-field diagnostic for this case, confirmed by reading both directly), and `computeImpact` (`pipeline.ts`) to confirm it's a genuinely separate, pre-build "lost fields/stricter rules" impact-preview mechanism, not the right place for this fix (correctly left untouched).

**`apps/api/src/codegen.ts` already has its own, stronger mitigation**: the exported standalone app's own `relationResolvable`/`requiredUnsupported` (the established pattern from rounds 798/851/852/855's file-field work) already blocks creating or editing a record with a required relation field pointing at a nonexistent entity, entirely, in the exported app's own UI -- a hard UI block, stronger than this round's advisory-only migration-layer note. No parity fix needed; confirmed by reading the relevant `codegen.ts` lines directly rather than assuming "codegen.ts always needs porting."

**The tests**: a new `migrate.test.ts` test covering all three new-column/table paths, each paired with the identical scenario using an OPTIONAL relation field instead -- confirming the required-only scoping genuinely holds (the deliberate placeholder pattern stays silent in every one of them, not just the one domain-library example).

**Verification**: confirmed failing cleanly without the fix -- the very-first-build case produced no `relation_missing_fk` entry at all where one was expected -- via a `git stash push -- packages/db/src/migrate.ts` / run / `git stash pop` cycle, and passing with the fix restored. Full `migrate.test.ts` (41 tests), `@forge/db` (219 tests), `@forge/spec-engine` (163 tests -- specifically re-run to confirm no regression of the exact suite round 415's own revert caught the original conflict in; this fix's non-blocking, required-only design never touches that path at all), and `apps/api` (448 tests, every file except the SIGKILL-prone `codegen.test.ts`) all ran clean. `apps/api`'s build ran clean.

**Status**: shipped and pushed, `packages/db/src/migrate.ts` only.

### Round 861: session tokens were stored and looked up as raw, directly-replayable plaintext -- the one bearer-style secret in this app that never got the hash-at-rest treatment its own two siblings already have

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey re-examined `packages/db/src/users.ts`'s `sessions` table against `routes/auth.ts`'s own established, heavily-documented convention for its other secrets, and found the one secret that matters most was the one exception.

**The gap**: `sessions` (`CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS sessions (token TEXT PRIMARY KEY, userId TEXT NOT NULL, expiresAt TEXT NOT NULL)`) stored the session token exactly as `issueSession` generated it (`randomBytes(32).toString("hex")`), with `createSession`/`getSessionUser`/`deleteSession`/`deleteOtherSessionsForUser` all reading and writing it as a raw string, no transformation at all. This is the one credential actually used on every single authenticated API request, valid for up to 30 days (`SESSION_TTL_MS`) -- the longest-lived secret in the whole app.

**Why this stood out immediately**: this exact codebase already identified and fixed this precise risk class for its two OTHER bearer-style secrets, in the very same file. `hashResetToken`'s own doc comment: "The token itself is never stored -- only this hash -- so a DB leak alone can't be replayed into a password reset **the same way a leaked session token could**." `hashLoginCode`'s own doc comment: "...can't be replayed into a login **the way a leaked session token could**." Both comments explicitly name the session-token risk as the thing they're protecting against for their own secret -- written with full awareness that the session token itself had this exact weakness, yet nothing ever went back to close it. No comment anywhere in `users.ts`/`auth.ts` frames this as a deliberate trade-off, unlike every other security decision in this codebase (each heavily commented with its own rationale), which is itself the signal that this was an oversight, not a choice.

**Why this is reachable, not theoretical**: anything that exposes a row from the `sessions` table hands an attacker a ready-to-use, 30-day-valid credential for that exact user, no cracking required -- a DB admin's read access (a legitimate but higher-privilege role than "can log in as any user"), a future read-only diagnostics/reporting feature that happens to touch this table, a verbose logger or APM tool capturing bound SQL parameters, or a leaked/stolen SQLite file (a single file, trivially copyable). This is the standard "token theft via data-at-rest exposure" risk class, and it's exactly the risk this codebase already reasoned about and mitigated for the two shorter-lived secrets in the identical login flow.

**The fix**: added `hashSessionToken` (sha256, matching `hashResetToken`/`hashLoginCode`'s own deliberate choice of a fast hash over `hashPassword`'s scrypt -- a session token's real defense is its 256 bits of randomness plus its TTL, not hash cost, the identical reasoning those two already use), applied inside `createSession`/`getSessionUser`/`deleteSession`/`deleteOtherSessionsForUser` -- fully encapsulated in `packages/db/src/users.ts` itself, so every caller (`routes/auth.ts`'s `issueSession`/logout/change-password/delete-account, `auth/middleware.ts`'s `requireAuth`) keeps passing the plaintext token exactly as before, with zero call-site changes needed anywhere outside this one file. This is a stronger guarantee than the sibling pattern (which depends on every caller in `routes/auth.ts` remembering to hash before writing) -- here the invariant is owned entirely by the DB layer, impossible to forget at a future call site.

**Two existing tests needed updating, caught by directly running the suite rather than assuming success**: one asserted the raw token string appeared in the stored `token` column directly (now compares against `hashSessionToken`'s own output); one raw-SQL-inserted a plaintext token specifically to isolate `getSessionUser`'s expiry-filter behavior from `createSession`'s own opportunistic pruning -- after the fix, that test would have still PASSED, but for the wrong reason (a hash mismatch, not the expiry check it's named for), so it was fixed to insert the matching hash and keep testing what it actually claims to.

**The test**: a new `users.test.ts` test confirming the actual security property directly -- the stored row never holds the plaintext token (`assert.notEqual`, plus an exact-match check against `hashSessionToken`'s own output so a no-op "transformation" couldn't slip through), while a real session is still correctly found by `getSessionUser` using the original plaintext (proving the lookup side hashes consistently, not just the write side).

**Verification**: confirmed failing cleanly without the fix -- a module-load `SyntaxError` (`hashSessionToken` not yet exported), the same "module-load crash = strong confirmation" signal this routine has relied on repeatedly -- via a `git stash push -- packages/db/src/users.ts` / run / `git stash pop` cycle, and passing with the fix restored. Full `users.test.ts` (13 tests), `@forge/db` (220 tests), and `apps/api` (448 tests, every file except the SIGKILL-prone `codegen.test.ts` -- including every real HTTP login/logout/change-password/delete-account integration test, confirming zero observable behavior change from `routes/auth.ts`'s own perspective) all ran clean. `apps/api`'s build ran clean.

**One real-world consequence, called out explicitly rather than left implicit**: every session token already stored as plaintext before this deploys will no longer match the new hashed lookup, so every currently-signed-in user on the real deployment will need to log in again once -- a one-time, expected, self-resolving cost of this security improvement, the same category as a password-hashing-scheme upgrade. Flagged clearly in the round's closing summary to שלומי rather than treated as a silent side effect.

**Status**: shipped and pushed, `packages/db/src/users.ts` only -- `apps/api/src/codegen.ts` (the exported standalone app) has no auth system of its own at all, so there is no sibling to port this to.

### Round 863: a required relation field that survives a refine unchanged still got no hazard note when its own target entity was removed -- the mirror-image of round 860's own fix, one step later in a field's life

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey was explicitly steered away from the rate-limiting/SSRF/session-storage territory of rounds 857-862 and back into `migrate.ts`'s own relation-handling logic, finding a genuine second half of round 860's own fix that round 860 itself didn't reach.

**The gap**: round 860 closed the case where a relation field is CREATED with an unresolvable `relationTo` (the `new_table`/`new_column` branches). The `prevField`-relation branch (the one that handles a field surviving UNCHANGED across a refine) never got the equivalent check: its own `expectedFkTable` is computed as `field.relationTo && entityNames.has(field.relationTo) ? tableNameFor(...) : undefined`, and BOTH of its existing conditions (`relation_target_changed`, and the original `relation_missing_fk` for a target that resolves but lost its physical FK) require `expectedFkTable` to be truthy. When a refine removes the target entity entirely while leaving the relation field itself completely untouched, `expectedFkTable` becomes `undefined` and neither condition can ever be true -- zero hazard reported, for a required field whose target just vanished from the live spec.

**Confirmed empirically, not just read**: built a real `Driver`/`Order.driverId` relation (required, `relationTo: "Driver"`), confirmed a genuine FK via `PRAGMA foreign_key_list` (`driverId -> entity_proj1_Driver`), then ran `diffAndMigrate` against a next spec with `Driver` removed and `driverId` byte-for-byte unchanged. Result: `changes` was `[]`. Additive-only migration never drops the physical table or its FK -- the column keeps pointing at a real table that's simply invisible anywhere in the current spec, with the field still required and still rejecting an empty value.

**The fix**: a third branch alongside the prevField-relation branch's existing two, firing when `field.required && field.relationTo && !entityNames.has(field.relationTo)` -- the identical required-only scoping round 860 already established as the distinguishing mechanism round 415's own revert note demanded (an optional relation field losing its target this way is `domainEntities.ts`'s own deliberate "not assigned to anything real" placeholder shape, just reached by removal instead of never having existed). ### Round 864: AutomationsPanel's own Entity dropdown and rule-list text never disambiguated two entities sharing a label -- the one surface its own sibling field-label fix (round 770) and `checkpointDiff.ts`'s own existing entity-level pair never reached

Still no genuine reply from שלומי. This round's survey returned to `AutomationsPanel.tsx` itself -- the same file round 770 already hardened for a FIELD sharing a label across two entities -- and found the identical risk shape one level up, at the ENTITY itself, never closed.

**The gap**: the create-form's entity `<select>` rendered each option as a bare `entity.label ?? entity.name`, and `describeRule`'s own rule-list text resolved a rule's stored `entityName` back to a display string via a local `entityLabel(rule)` helper that did the same bare lookup. Neither disambiguated two entities sharing a label. The Entity Label editor enforces no uniqueness at all -- `routes/projects.ts`'s `PATCH /entities/:entityName/label` accepts any non-empty string with zero collision check against sibling entities -- so an ordinary owner can trigger this through the already-shipped UI alone: rename two different entities (e.g. an active-customers table and an archived-customers table) to the same label, "Customer."

**Why this is worse than it looks at first**: the create-form dropdown showing two identical-looking rows is merely confusing -- the real damage is in the rule LIST. `describeRule`'s text ("When a 'Customer' record is created...") is this panel's entire reason to exist: a reviewer scanning existing automation rules has no other way to tell which rule does what. With two same-labeled entities, an existing rule's own description gave zero way to tell which of the two it actually targets -- directly undermining the one thing this panel is for.

**The misleading signal that nearly hid this**: the file's own doc comment, sitting directly above the pre-existing field-label-disambiguation helpers, claimed entities were "already disambiguated" -- but reading it carefully, and reading `checkpointDiff.ts`'s own comment it referenced, showed that claim was about FIELD labels needing their own separate per-entity scoping, never about entity labels themselves. Confirmed by direct code reading, not by trusting the comment's framing, per this routine's own repeatedly-reinforced lesson against assuming a sibling gap is already covered just because a nearby comment implies it.

**The fix, mirroring not importing per established convention**: `checkpointDiff.ts` already has its own `entityLabelOccurrences`/`entityDisplayLabel` pair for the identical purpose, with its own explicit comment stating this helper pair is deliberately mirrored (not imported) into each consuming surface, citing `pipeline.ts`'s own original copy as precedent. Added the identical pair locally to `AutomationsPanel.tsx`, wired into both the create-form's entity `<select>` and `entityLabel(rule)`, which `describeRule` already calls for every rule-list description -- so the fix reaches both the picker and the existing-rule text with one change. Confirmed via grep that no other raw entity-label rendering site exists in this file.

**The test**: a new `AutomationsPanel.test.ts` test with two entities (`CustomerActive`/`CustomerArchived`) both labeled "Customer" and one existing rule targeting the archived one -- asserting the dropdown's option text reads `["Customer (CustomerActive)", "Customer (CustomerArchived)"]`, and that the rule list's own description names "Customer (CustomerArchived)" specifically, not the bare ambiguous label.

**Verification**: confirmed failing cleanly without the fix -- the dropdown's option text came back as `["Customer", "Customer"]`, indistinguishable -- via a `git stash push -- apps/web/src/AutomationsPanel.tsx` / run / `git stash pop` cycle, and passing with the fix restored.
